  2835  E. Part 351, Subpart F: Furloughs, Abolishment of Competitive Area, 
  2836  USERRA Rights, and Exceptions
  2837  
  2838      OPM is modifying Sec.  351.601 for consistency with how retention 
  2839  standing is to be calculated under Subpart E of part 351. OPM is also 
  2840  modifying Sec.  351.602 to remove the prohibition on retaining an 
  2841  employee serving a specifically limited temporary appointment in a 
  2842  competitive level while releasing a competing employee from that level. 
  2843  OPM did not receive significant adverse comments on these provisions 
  2844  and is finalizing them.
  2845  1. RIF Furloughs
  2846      In the proposed rule, OPM proposed to modify its regulations in 
  2847  Sec.  351.604 regarding furloughs of more than 30 consecutive calendar 
  2848  days (or more than 22 workdays if done on a discontinuous basis over a 
  2849  period not exceeding 1 year) to remove the requirement that agencies 
  2850  furlough employees based on retention standing and recall employees to 
  2851  duty from furlough based on retention standing.
  2852      Commenter 0687 opposed these changes, contending that they had ``no 
  2853  obvious use case and could create mechanisms for abuse.'' Commenter 
  2854  0687 noted that agencies typically do not engage in unpaid furloughs of 
  2855  any length, whether greater or less than 30 days, and that OPM's 
  2856  proposed revision would create risks that agencies could use long 
  2857  furloughs to circumvent normal RIF procedures. Commenter 0687 therefore 
  2858  contended that the risks of this new provision outweigh the benefits. 
  2859  Commenter 0117 similarly expressed concern that agencies could use 
  2860  long-term unpaid furloughs to avoid following retention order 
  2861  requirements. OPM agrees that its proposed changes to Sec.  351.604 
  2862  warrant further consideration and has chosen not to finalize them.
  2863  2. Abolishment of a Competitive Area
  2864      In this rule, OPM is renaming Sec.  351.605 as Abolishment of a 
  2865  competitive area to more accurately describe its purpose. The revised 
  2866  section explains that the appropriate use of this provision is when an 
  2867  agency is abolishing all positions (including the positions of 
  2868  employees otherwise excluded from RIF competition under Sec.  
  2869  351.202(d)) in a competitive area within 180 days. It further explains 
  2870  that, because all positions in the competitive area will be eliminated, 
  2871  an agency is not required to release competing employees in order of 
  2872  retention standing.
  2873      As the D.C. Circuit explained in upholding an earlier version of 
  2874  this provision, when all employees in a competitive area will be 
  2875  released within a relatively short time, ``it is certainly reasonable 
  2876  to conclude that it would be a waste of resources for an agency to be 
  2877  forced to perform detailed seniority and performance calculations 
  2878  solely to construct a rank ordering of employees' retention rights when 
  2879  those rights are of such little value.'' AFGE v. OPM, 821 F.2d at 766 
  2880  n. 4. Thus, OPM was ``within its authority to conclude that under those 
  2881  limited circumstances, no effect is `due.' '' Id. With performance now 
  2882  the main consideration governing RIF retention, the same considerations 
  2883  apply: it does not make sense to require agencies to perform detailed 
  2884  seniority and performance calculations to construct a rank ordering of 
  2885  employees that will have no substantive effect on their retention 
  2886  rights.
  2887      In this final rule, OPM is making minor wording and ordering 
  2888  changes to this provision. Section 351.605(c) provides that any 
  2889  competing employee released under this provision must be provided a 
  2890  specific written notice in accordance with Sec.  351.801, Notice 
  2891  period. The notice must include the following: the action being taken 
  2892  and its effective date; the competitive area being abolished; a link to 
  2893  5 CFR part 351 and access to the agency's records pertinent to the RIF 
  2894  being run to abolish the competitive area; information on reemployment 
  2895  rights; the employee's appeal rights; and a statement that, because all 
  2896  positions in the competitive area are being abolished pursuant to 5 CFR 
  2897  351.605, the employee was not ranked relative to other competing 
  2898  employees in the reduction in force. The notice is not required to 
  2899  include the information described in Sec.  351.802(a)(2) or (a)(4).
  2900      Section 351.605(d), Retention register not required, explains that 
  2901  an agency is not required to rank competing employees in the abolished 
  2902  competitive area, and must not apply the assignment right provisions in 
  2903  subpart G, because
  2904  
  2905  [[Page 49203]]
  2906  
  2907  no positions in the competitive area will remain.
  2908      Commenter 0683 suggested that OPM review and approve any 
  2909  competitive area abolishment due to the potential that agencies could 
  2910  use this provision alongside the new competitive area definition to 
  2911  evade the need to build a retention register and provide assignment 
  2912  rights. OPM believes that these concerns are adequately addressed by 
  2913  the requirement in Sec.  351.402(c) that OPM approve new or 
  2914  substantially modified competitive areas that have been in effect less 
  2915  than 90 days prior to the issuance of RIF notices; the requirement in 
  2916  Sec.  351.204 that agencies must administer and apply the regulations 
  2917  consistent with all applicable laws, including the Merit System 
  2918  Principles in 5 U.S.C. 2301(b); the requirement that the competitive 
  2919  area be disclosed to the employee in the RIF notice; and the 
  2920  availability of RIF appeal rights in Subpart I of 5 CFR part 351.
  2921      Commenter 0683 also asked that OPM clarify that the abolishment of 
  2922  a competitive area under Section 351.605 does not diminish or supersede 
  2923  the statutory placement rights of career SES members under 5 U.S.C. 
  2924  3594-3595. OPM confirms that these revisions are not intended to 
  2925  diminish or supersede career SES placement rights in a RIF. However, 
  2926  OPM believes that 5 CFR 359.602(b) is clear enough on this point that 
  2927  no change to the regulatory text in 5 CFR part 351 is required.
  2928  3. USERRA Rights
  2929      In the proposed rule, OPM proposed to modify Sec.  351.606(a), 
  2930  which addresses mandatory RIF exceptions for employees who have been 
  2931  restored or reemployed following uniformed service and who remain 
  2932  entitled to post-reemployment retention protection under Sec.  
  2933  353.209(b) for either 6 months or 1 year. These retention rights are 
  2934  provided under USERRA.
  2935      Commenter 0686, a Federal agency, requested that OPM clarify the 
  2936  proposed modifications to Sec.  351.606, and particularly its 
  2937  interaction with Sec.  351.605, which revises the procedures to be 
  2938  followed when a competitive area is abolished. Several other commenters 
  2939  (0076, 0121, 0455, 0550, 0597) argued that the proposed rule could be 
  2940  read as undermining USERRA rights, including where an employee 
  2941  performing uniformed service or recently reemployed after uniformed 
  2942  service lacks recent civilian performance ratings.
  2943      OPM agrees that clarification is appropriate. Accordingly, OPM in 
  2944  this final rule is making explicit how USERRA restoration and retention 
  2945  protections operate when an employee is affected by a RIF.
  2946      First, OPM is adding a definition of ``Restoration protected 
  2947  employee'' in Sec.  351.203. For purposes of part 351, a restoration 
  2948  protected employee is a competing employee who has been restored or 
  2949  reemployed following uniformed service and who, as of the date the 
  2950  employee receives a specific reduction in force notice, remains within 
  2951  the 6-month or 1-year post-reemployment protection period described in 
  2952  Sec.  353.209(b). Those protection periods implement 38 U.S.C. 4316(c), 
  2953  which provides that a person reemployed under USERRA may not be 
  2954  discharged from employment, except for cause, for 1 year after 
  2955  reemployment if the period of uniformed service was more than 180 days, 
  2956  or for 180 days after reemployment if the period of service was more 
  2957  than 30 days but less than 181 days.
  2958      Second, OPM is revising Sec.  351.606 to clarify that agencies must 
  2959  apply USERRA retention protections and restoration rights as a 
  2960  mandatory exception to the ordinary RIF order of release. The agency 
  2961  must first determine the employee's ordinary retention standing under 
  2962  subpart E. The agency must then apply the mandatory exception in Sec.  
  2963  351.606(a). During the applicable 6-month or 1-year protection period, 
  2964  the agency may not release a restoration protected employee from the 
  2965  competitive level if another competing employee may be released 
  2966  instead.
  2967      Third, OPM is clarifying how the mandatory exception applies when 
  2968  an agency abolishes all positions in a competitive area under Sec.  
  2969  351.605. When an entire competitive area is abolished pursuant to Sec.  
  2970  351.605, the agency may not separate the restoration protected employee 
  2971  by RIF during the applicable 6-month or 1-year protection period. 
  2972  Instead, the employee must be assigned by the agency to a different 
  2973  position of like seniority, status, and pay for which the employee is 
  2974  qualified, consistent with 5 CFR part 353.
  2975      Fourth, OPM is revising Sec.  353.209(a) to conform part 353 to 
  2976  these part 351 clarifications. Section 353.209(a) already provides that 
  2977  an employee performing duty with the uniformed services may not be 
  2978  demoted or separated, other than military separation, except for cause; 
  2979  that RIF is not ``for cause'' under that subpart; that the employee is 
  2980  not a competing employee under part 351; and that, if the employee's 
  2981  position is abolished during the absence, the agency must reassign the 
  2982  employee to another position of like status and pay. OPM is clarifying 
  2983  that this reassignment obligation applies when the employee's position 
  2984  is abolished in a RIF, including when all positions in the employee's 
  2985  competitive area are abolished under Sec.  351.605.
  2986      Fifth, OPM is clarifying the relationship between part 351, part 
  2987  353, and 38 U.S.C. 4314 when the employing agency can no longer place 
  2988  the employee. If the employee's function has been transferred to 
  2989  another agency, the employee's rights are governed by the transfer and 
  2990  restoration provisions in 5 CFR part 353. If the employing agency no 
  2991  longer exists and its functions have not been transferred, or if it is 
  2992  impossible or unreasonable for the agency to reassign the restoration 
  2993  protected employee, OPM will offer placement assistance elsewhere in 
  2994  the executive branch to the employee pursuant to 5 CFR 353.110.
  2995      These revisions also address concerns that employees performing 
  2996  uniformed service, or recently returned from uniformed service, may 
  2997  lack recent civilian ratings of record. This rule's missing-rating 
  2998  provisions continue to address how ordinary performance credit is 
  2999  calculated for competing employees who do not have three ratings of 
  3000  record, including use of the modal rating for employees with no ratings 
  3001  during the relevant four-year period and proxy rules for employees with 
  3002  one or two ratings. But for a restoration-protected employee within the 
  3003  6-month or 1-year post-reemployment protection period, the mandatory 
  3004  exception in Sec.  351.606(a) operates independently of the employee's 
  3005  ordinary retention standing. Thus, the employee is not penalized for 
  3006  lacking recent civilian ratings during the protected period; the agency 
  3007  must honor the USERRA retention protection before releasing the 
  3008  employee by RIF.
  3009      In addition, this rule preserves credit for uniformed service in 
  3010  calculating length of service for RIF purposes. Section 351.505(b)(1) 
  3011  provides that all active duty in a uniformed service, as defined in 5 
  3012  U.S.C. 2101(3), is creditable for purposes of part 351, except as 
  3013  otherwise provided in that section. The service computation date 
  3014  includes all actual creditable service under Sec.  351.505(a) and (b).
  3015  4. Exceptions
  3016      OPM is modifying and clarifying current Sec.  351.607, relabeling 
  3017  this section as Discretionary continuing exceptions to harmonize this 
  3018  section with other provisions in this chapter for which agency use is 
  3019  optional. OPM is also modifying and clarifying Sec.  351.608, renaming 
  3020  this section Discretionary

  3023  
  3024  temporary exceptions. OPM is also creating new flexibilities for an

summary.text:
**Comparing regulatory language**

I’m identifying possible discrepancies between the explanatory preamble and the regulatory text. One strong mismatch is that the preamble describes a “specifically limited temporary appointment” in a competitive level, while §351.602(a) refers to a “specifically limited temporary or term promotion.” The later regulatory language also consistently uses “promotion,” which strengthens the concern.

I’m also checking §351.605: the preamble says notice content includes information about reemployment rights, while §351.605(c) instead cross-references §351.802(a)(5), (a)(6), and (b).**Checking remaining discrepancies**

I’m reviewing whether the cross-reference in §351.605 accurately captures reemployment-priority information; it likely does, because §351.802 appears to address the relevant priority details.

Most other differences seem non-substantive. The preamble’s wording about being “reemployed” versus the regulation’s “restored” appears synonymous, while the regulation provides additional conditions rather than contradicting the summary. Likewise, the discussion of sick leave is broadly consistent: available sick leave must be used before other appropriate leave.

I’m scrutinizing §351.608 next, especially whether describing military-spouse leave as “up to 90 days” oversimplifies varied limits.

**Clarifying parental leave timing**

I’m parsing how the rule handles children born or placed for adoption around the effective date. The key distinction seems to be whether the birth or placement occurred before the reduction-in-force rules took effect, rather than simply calling the child “recently born.” I’m also noting the separate provision for an employee or employee’s spouse who is pregnant on the effective date. Paid parental leave may continue for an eligible pre-effective-date birth or placement until the available leave is exhausted.**Checking regulatory consistency**

I’m cataloging precise differences between the preamble and regulatory text rather than broad similarities. One possible issue is the description of restoration rights, which may overstate mandatory retention protection after restoration. I’m also comparing terminology about competitive-area changes, including “substantially modified” versus “materially modifies,” and checking whether the required submission timing matches. Other points include the tenure-subgroup date, temporary versus term promotions, qualification lookback periods, leave-coverage conditions, and whether the furlough proposal was ultimately omitted.

  1540  
  1541      OPM responds to comments regarding specific sections of this rule 
  1542  below.
  1543  
  1544  A. Part 351, Subpart B: Changes in Definitions, Coverage, Use of 
  1545  Regulations, and Agency Responsibilities
  1546  
  1547  1. Erosion of Duties Reclassifications
  1548      OPM is modifying Sec.  351.201(a)(2) to remove from the list of 
  1549  actions that require agencies to use RIF procedures reclassification of 
  1550  an employee's position due to erosion of duties if the action would 
  1551  take effect after an agency had formally announced a RIF in the 
  1552  employee's competitive area and the RIF would take effect within 180 
  1553  days.
  1554      Commenter 0532 argued that OPM has not justified removing erosion-
  1555  of-duties reclassifications from the actions requiring RIF procedures. 
  1556  OPM disagrees.
  1557      The proposed rule explains the history of the erosion-of-duties 
  1558  provision. In 1986, OPM generally removed erosion-of-duties 
  1559  reclassifications from the categories of actions subject to RIF 
  1560  procedures, but retained a narrow RIF-procedure requirement for 
  1561  reclassifications occurring after announcement of a RIF and within 180 
  1562  days of the RIF effective date. OPM is now removing that narrow 
  1563  procedural trigger because it is unreasonable and impracticable to 
  1564  require agencies to build a retention register for such 
  1565  reclassifications, and OPM is not aware of any agency actually 
  1566  executing an erosion-of-duties reclassification action using RIF 
  1567  procedures since the 1986 revision.
  1568      Commenter 0037 argued that the ``erosion of duties'' changes could 
  1569  be used to constructively demote disfavored employees. OPM disagrees. 
  1570  Erosion of duties reclassifications have generally been excluded from 
  1571  RIF procedures since 1986, except in the narrow circumstance where the 
  1572  reclassification will take effect after an agency has formally 
  1573  announced a RIF in the employee's competitive area that will take 
  1574  effect within 180 days. This rule directly addresses concerns that 
  1575  erosion-of-duties reclassifications could be used to undermine the RIF 
  1576  retention order. Rather than requiring a full RIF process for erosion-
  1577  of-duties reclassifications, this rule will bar agencies from 
  1578  undertaking an erosion-of-duties reclassification between the formal 
  1579  announcement and completion of a RIF if the action would adversely 
  1580  affect an employee's retention standing in the RIF. This is a more 
  1581  direct and administrable safeguard than the current rule. Notably, 
  1582  commenters 0037 and 0532 do not identify any concrete instance in which 
  1583  the existing erosion-of-duties RIF trigger has been necessary to 
  1584  protect employees, nor do
  1585  
  1586  [[Page 49191]]
  1587  
  1588  commenters 0037 or 0532 explain why the proposed anti-manipulation 
  1589  prohibition would be inadequate.
  1590      Instead, OPM agrees with Commenter 0720, a Federal agency, that the 
  1591  current erosion-of-duties provision is outdated, and OPM's approach in 
  1592  this rule ``reduces unnecessary confusion and risk while preserving 
  1593  safeguards against improper alterations to retention outcomes.''
  1594  2. Employees Excluded From RIF Competition
  1595      This rule modifies the definition of the term Competing employee in 
  1596  Sec.  351.203 to mean an employee in the competitive service tenure 
  1597  group or the excepted service tenure group. It also adds a definition 
  1598  of Competitive service tenure group to mean all employees within 
  1599  competitive service tenure subgroups I and II; that is, all employees 
  1600  in the competitive service who, as of the date of the RIF notice, are 
  1601  not serving an initial probationary period or a temporary appointment 
  1602  of 1 year or less under subpart D of 5 CFR part 316. This rule defines 
  1603  the Excepted service tenure group as all employees within excepted 
  1604  service tenure subgroups I and II; that is, all excepted service 
  1605  appointees serving in a career position (that is, not in Schedule C or 
  1606  G) who, as of the date of the RIF notice, are not serving a trial 
  1607  period or in a temporary or time-limited appointment of 1 year or less.
  1608      OPM is also adding definitions of initial probationary period and 
  1609  trial period to Sec.  351.203. With respect to these provisions, OPM 
  1610  notes that a supervisory or managerial employee with career tenure who 
  1611  is only on probation with respect to those supervisory or managerial 
  1612  functions (i.e., is entitled to be returned to a nonsupervisory or non-
  1613  managerial position rather than being subject to removal under 5 CFR 
  1614  part 315, subpart I) would be included in the RIF in the supervisory or 
  1615  managerial position, and would not be subject to the exclusion from RIF 
  1616  procedures applicable to individuals serving an initial probationary 
  1617  period under 5 CFR 11.2. Further, an employee who is serving both an 
  1618  initial probationary period and a supervisory probationary period 
  1619  simultaneously is exempt from RIF procedures.
  1620      In the proposed rule, OPM proposed to add a Sec.  351.202(d) that 
  1621  lists categories of employees excluded from RIF retention procedures, 
  1622  as they fall outside the definition of ``competing employees'' under 5 
  1623  U.S.C. 3502(a). Under OPM's definition of ``competing employees,'' 
  1624  employees in the competitive service who are serving an initial 
  1625  probationary period would be excluded from RIF procedures, as would 
  1626  employees in the excepted service who are serving a trial period. In 
  1627  addition, competitive and excepted service employees who are serving 
  1628  temporary or time-limited appointments of 1 year or less would be 
  1629  excluded from RIF competition, as would Schedule C and Schedule G 
  1630  employees.
  1631      In this final rule, OPM is revising the wording of Sec.  
  1632  351.202(d). The revised wording narrows Sec.  351.202(d) from a broad 
  1633  statement that certain employees are excluded from part 351 altogether 
  1634  to a more precise statement that they are not ``competing employees'' 
  1635  for RIF purposes. The final rule clarifies the consequences of this 
  1636  classification: an agency may retain such an employee while releasing a 
  1637  competing employee, and may furlough, separate, demote, or reassign 
  1638  such an employee for a reason described in Sec.  351.201(a)(2) (lack of 
  1639  work, shortage of funds, insufficient personnel ceiling, 
  1640  reorganization, or the exercise of reemployment rights or restoration 
  1641  rights) without determining the employee's retention standing under 
  1642  subparts D and E, applying the order-of-release provisions in subpart 
  1643  F, or providing assignment rights under subpart G, provided the action 
  1644  is otherwise consistent with the terms of the employee's appointment 
  1645  and applicable law. Further, the revised text clarifies that these 
  1646  excluded employees are still subject to the notice provisions of Sec.  
  1647  351.801 where they are furloughed for more than 30 days, separated, 
  1648  demoted, or reassigned for the reasons described in Sec.  
  1649  351.201(a)(2), and the action is not merely the expiration of a 
  1650  temporary or time-limited appointment according to its terms. Under 
  1651  such circumstances the agency must provide the employee a modified 
  1652  written notice that includes the action to be taken, the reasons for 
  1653  the action, and its effective date; a link to 5 CFR part 351 and access 
  1654  to the agency's records pertinent to the reduction in force being 
  1655  taken; information on reemployment rights; and any appeal rights.
  1656      In addition, the final rule makes other wording changes to Sec.  
  1657  351.202(d). It revises the Schedule C and Schedule G language by 
  1658  referring to employees ``serving under'' those appointments and removes 
  1659  a proposed reference to term appointments under part 316 subpart C, 
  1660  making clear that the competitive-service temporary-appointment 
  1661  exclusion is limited to temporary appointments of 1 year or less under 
  1662  part 316 subpart D.
  1663      Commenter 0719, a Federal agency, supported the proposed changes 
  1664  excluding initial probationary period and trial period employees from 
  1665  RIF competition, noting that the current RIF rules demand that 
  1666  probationary and trial period employees be released first in a RIF. 
  1667  Commenter 0719 noted that this results in ``the loss of high potential 
  1668  individuals essential for long term succession planning and mission 
  1669  continuity.'' The agency noted that ``[r]emoving these groups from RIF 
  1670  competition will allow [it] greater flexibility to retain high 
  1671  potential early career employees even in constrained budget 
  1672  conditions.'' Commenter 0687 noted that termination of probationary 
  1673  employees as part of workforce reshaping activities can ``weaken[] 
  1674  early career pipelines'' and result in the loss of some of the agency's 
  1675  ``best talent.'' OPM agrees.
  1676      Commenter 0678 claimed that these exclusions would mean that the 
  1677  RIF regulations would no longer provide a comprehensive system to 
  1678  govern workforce reductions, while Commenter 0684 argued that this 
  1679  change would conflict with 5 U.S.C. 3501(b)'s broad coverage provision. 
  1680  OPM disagrees. OPM has long used its authority under 5 U.S.C. 3502 to 
  1681  define the otherwise-undefined statutory term ``competing employees'' 
  1682  subject to RIF competition to exclude certain groups of employees from 
  1683  RIF retention procedures. For example, in its regulations at 5 CFR 
  1684  316.911, OPM recognizes that employees ``whose initial appointment [is] 
  1685  for a period of 1 year or less are not assigned a tenure group and do 
  1686  not compete with other employees in a RIF.'' In its regulations at 5 
  1687  CFR 353.209, OPM stated that an employee performing duty with the 
  1688  uniformed services ``is not a `competing employee' under'' the RIF 
  1689  regulations. And OPM's regulations at 5 CFR 351.705 have long provided 
  1690  that an agency may, but is not required to, provide assignment rights 
  1691  to excepted service employees.
  1692      Related statutory provisions, and the broader history of 
  1693  probationary and trial periods in the Federal service, support OPM's 
  1694  determination that probationary and trial period employees should not 
  1695  be considered ``competing employees'' for purposes of 5 U.S.C. 3502. 
  1696  The phrase ``competing employee'' in 5 U.S.C. 3502 must be read against 
  1697  a long background tracing to the Pendleton Act of 1883 whereby Congress 
  1698  has consistently and deliberately maintained a distinction between 
  1699  employees whose appointments have become final and employees still 
  1700  serving a probationary or trial period. This distinction reflects a 
  1701  longstanding congressional and regulatory judgment that competitive 
  1702  selection alone is not the final test of fitness for Federal
  1703  
  1704  [[Page 49192]]
  1705  
  1706  service. Rather, an initial period of actual service has always served 
  1707  as the Government's final opportunity to determine whether an employee 
  1708  should receive the full procedural protections associated with 
  1709  continuing Federal employment.
  1710      The Pendleton Act (22 Stat. 403) required that the ``there shall be 
  1711  a period of probation before any absolute appointment or employment 
  1712  aforesaid.'' That statutory formulation indicates that Congress did not 
  1713  treat appointment and final appointment as the same event. It preserved 
  1714  a two-step process--competitive appointment first, with final 
  1715  appointment only after satisfactory completion of probation.
  1716      In its first annual report in 1884, the Civil Service Commission 
  1717  characterized the probationary period as lasting ``six months before 
  1718  any absolute appointment can be made. At the end of this time the 
  1719  appointee goes out of the service unless then reappointed.'' \7\ Two 
  1720  years later, the Commission wrote in its third annual report that 
  1721  ``doing the public work is precisely what the Merit System provides. If 
  1722  at its termination the appointing officer is not . . . willing to make 
  1723  an unconditional appointment, the probationer is . . . absolutely out 
  1724  of the service without any action on the part of the Government.'' \8\
  1725  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1726  
  1727      \7\ First Annual Report of the United States Civil Service 
  1728  Commission to the President (1884), p. 29, https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=nnc1.cu09006737&seq=9.
  1729      \8\ Third Annual Report of the United States Civil Service 
  1730  Commission to the President (1886), p. 36, https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=njp.32101073361022&seq=40.
  1731  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1732  
  1733      With the enactment of the Lloyd-La Follette Act of 1912, Congress 
  1734  created the first legislative codification of protection against 
  1735  removal for civil servants. The Act established ``[t]hat no person in 
  1736  the classified civil service of the United States shall be removed 
  1737  therefrom except for such cause as will promote the efficiency of said 
  1738  service.'' \9\ The Act also imposed certain procedural requirements on 
  1739  removals including advance notice and an opportunity to respond in 
  1740  writing. However, Congress did not establish employment protections for 
  1741  probationary employees, and has maintained this exclusion through every 
  1742  subsequent recodification of the civil service laws.
  1743  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1744  
  1745      \9\ The Lloyd-La Follette Act, 37 Stat. 555 (1912), as amended, 
  1746  62 Stat. 354 (1948), 5 U.S.C.A. 652(a).
  1747  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1748  
  1749      Congress legislated against this backdrop in using the term 
  1750  ``competing employees'' in the Veterans' Preference Act of 1944 \10\--
  1751  the direct legislative predecessor of 5 U.S.C. 3502. The Veterans' 
  1752  Preference Act of 1944 did not define ``competing employees'' to 
  1753  include all individuals serving in Federal positions. Instead, Section 
  1754  12 of that Act provided that, in a reduction in personnel, ``competing 
  1755  employees'' would be released in accordance with Civil Service 
  1756  Commission regulations giving due effect to the statutory retention 
  1757  factors. Congress thus left the identification of the competitive group 
  1758  to regulation.
  1759  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1760  
  1761      \10\ Public Law 78-359, 58 Stat. 387 (codified, as amended in 
  1762  part, at 5 U.S.C. 3309-3320).
  1763  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1764  
  1765      This is particularly significant because, in Section 14, the 
  1766  Veterans' Preference Act expanded civil service protections to 
  1767  preference eligible Federal employees, but it explicitly excluded 
  1768  probationers, limiting its protections to a ``permanent or indefinite 
  1769  preference eligible, who has completed a probationary or trial 
  1770  period.'' Section 12 and section 14 were enacted in the same statute. 
  1771  If Congress believed probationary and trial-period employees 
  1772  necessarily had to be treated the same as final appointees for all 
  1773  retention-related purposes, it would be odd for Congress, two sections 
  1774  later, to condition major procedural protections on completion of 
  1775  probationary or trial service. The better reading is that the 1944 Act 
  1776  preserved a two-step civil-service model: an employee could enter 
  1777  Federal service and receive whatever preference rights the statute and 
  1778  regulations afforded, but the employee did not necessarily become part 
  1779  of the competitive retention workforce before completing the 
  1780  probationary or trial period.
  1781      The statutory text of 5 U.S.C. 3502(a) therefore does not compel 
  1782  OPM to include employees serving an initial probationary or trial 
  1783  period in RIF competition; rather, it permits OPM to determine by 
  1784  regulation that such employees are not ``competing employees'' for 
  1785  purposes of retention registers and order of release, while preserving 
  1786  any independently applicable statutory or regulatory protections.\11\
  1787  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1788  
  1789      \11\ Commenter 0684 points to Fathauer v. United States, 566 
  1790  F.3d 1352 (Fed. Cir. 2009), but that case is inapposite. Here, OPM 
  1791  is not defining ``employee'' in 5 U.S.C. 3501(b) to nullify 
  1792  statutory coverage. Instead, it is defining the narrower, undefined 
  1793  term ``competing employee'' in section 3502(a), a term Congress 
  1794  expressly left for implementation through OPM regulations.
  1795  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1796  
  1797      The current 5 U.S.C. 7511 codifies the longstanding exclusion of 
  1798  probationary and trial period employees from the adverse-action 
  1799  definition of ``employee.'' Under 5 U.S.C. 7511, an ``employee'' in the 
  1800  competitive service or excepted service generally means an individual 
  1801  who is not serving a probationary or trial period under an initial 
  1802  appointment or who has completed one year of current continuous service 
  1803  under other than a temporary appointment limited to one year or less.
  1804      Courts interpreting section 7511 and related CSRA provisions have 
  1805  repeatedly recognized that Congress intended agencies to retain 
  1806  substantial flexibility over probationary and trial-period employees. 
  1807  In Department of Justice v. FLRA, the D.C. Circuit relied on the CSRA's 
  1808  structure and legislative history in concluding that probationary 
  1809  employees could not obtain through negotiated grievance procedures the 
  1810  kind of review Congress deliberately withheld from them in chapter 
  1811  75.\12\ 709 F.2d 724, 730 (D.C. Cir. 1983). In United States v. 
  1812  Connolly, the Federal Circuit likewise treated the exclusion of 
  1813  probationary employees from chapter 75 appeal rights as a deliberate 
  1814  congressional choice, not a statutory gap for courts or agencies to 
  1815  fill.\13\ And in National Treasury Employees Union v. FLRA, the D.C. 
  1816  Circuit reaffirmed that the CSRA's treatment of probationary employees 
  1817  reflects Congress's judgment that agencies must have latitude to assess 
  1818  and separate employees who have not yet completed the testing period 
  1819  for Federal service.\14\ This history does not mean that section 7511 
  1820  directly controls chapter 35 RIF procedures. It does, however, confirm 
  1821  that OPM's treatment of probationary, trial-period, and short-term 
  1822  temporary employees in this rule is consistent with the broader civil-
  1823  service framework Congress enacted.
  1824  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1825  
  1826      \12\ See Dep't of Justice v. FLRA, 709 F.2d 724, 730 (D.C. Cir. 
  1827  1983).
  1828      \13\ See U.S. v. Connolly, 716 F.2d 882, 886 (Fed. Cir. 1983).
  1829      \14\ See Nat'l Treasury Emps. Union v. FLRA, 848 F.2d 1273, 1275 
  1830  (D.C. Cir. 1988).
  1831  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1832  
  1833      In addition, 5 U.S.C. 3502 should be read consistent with 5 U.S.C. 
  1834  3321, which contemplates a probationary period before an appointment 
  1835  becomes final and allows the President to issue rules and regulations 
  1836  effectuating probationary periods. Current Civil Service Rule 11, 
  1837  issued by the President under Executive Order (E.O.) 14284, already 
  1838  supplies a comprehensive framework for probationary and trial-period 
  1839  employment. It requires agencies to use probationary and trial periods 
  1840  to evaluate whether an employee's continuation in Federal service 
  1841  advances the public interest and expressly permits agencies to consider 
  1842  agency needs and interests, whether continued employment would advance 
  1843  agency or Government organizational goals, and whether continued
  1844  
  1845  [[Page 49193]]
  1846  
  1847  employment would advance the efficiency of the service.
  1848      Those considerations substantially overlap with the reasons 
  1849  agencies conduct RIFs, including lack of work, shortage of funds, and 
  1850  reorganization. Requiring agencies to apply full part 351 retention-
  1851  register, order-of-release, and assignment-right procedures to 
  1852  employees whose appointments have not yet become final would duplicate 
  1853  Rule 11 and could produce inconsistent outcomes. For example, Rule 11 
  1854  might support retaining a probationary employee because the employee 
  1855  has scarce skills, strong actual performance, and is needed for the 
  1856  agency's future mission. But a part 351 retention register would likely 
  1857  place the same employee low because the employee has little service 
  1858  time and may lack a rating of record. Thus, excluding probationary and 
  1859  trial period employees from the statutory definition of ``competing 
  1860  employees'' in 5 U.S.C. 3502(a) eliminates duplication and makes sense 
  1861  of the overall statutory scheme.
  1862      With respect to temporary employees, OPM's regulations at 5 CFR 
  1863  part 316, subpart D make clear that such appointments are only 
  1864  appropriate to meet short-term needs, including ``for such reasons as 
  1865  abolishment, reorganization, or contracting of the function, 
  1866  anticipated reduction in funding, or completion of a specific project 
  1867  or peak workload.'' 5 CFR 316.401(a)(2). Further, ``[t]he supervisor of 
  1868  each position filled by temporary appointment must certify that the 
  1869  employment need is truly temporary and that the proposed appointment 
  1870  meets the regulatory time limits.'' Id. 316.401(b). Thus, these 
  1871  regulations indicate that temporary employees do not have a reasonable 
  1872  expectation of long-term employment and thus should not be considered 
  1873  ``competing employees'' for purposes of 5 U.S.C. 3502.
  1874      Further, in the final rule, OPM has clarified that the employees 
  1875  excluded from RIF competition are not entirely outside the regulatory 
  1876  scheme and must receive a notice in accordance with 5 U.S.C. 3502(d) 
  1877  when they are furloughed for more than 30 days, separated, demoted, or 
  1878  reassigned for reasons of lack of work, shortage of funds, insufficient 
  1879  personnel ceiling, reorganization, or the exercise of reemployment 
  1880  rights or restoration rights and the action is not merely the 
  1881  expiration of a temporary or time-limited appointment according to its 
  1882  terms. In addition, the regulations provide in Sec.  351.605 that all 
  1883  positions in the competitive area, including those of employees 
  1884  excluded from RIF competition under Sec.  351.202(d), must be abolished 
  1885  within 180 days for an agency to permissibly use the streamlined 
  1886  procedures of that subpart.
  1887      Commenter 0672 objected that probationary employees can be covered 
  1888  by the proposal's missing-rating rules and therefore should remain in 
  1889  RIF competition. OPM does not agree that the proposed modal-rating 
  1890  provision eliminates the need to exclude probationary and trial-period 
  1891  employees from RIF competition. The modal-rating rule is a limited 
  1892  proxy for competing employees who lack ratings in the applicable 
  1893  lookback period; it does not provide an individualized measure of 
  1894  performance for employees whose appointments have not yet been 
  1895  finalized and who often have not served long enough to receive a rating 
  1896  of record. In a performance-first RIF system, assigning retention 
  1897  standing to such employees based on the most common rating assigned to 
  1898  other employees would fail to measure the employee's own performance. 
  1899  OPM therefore reasonably treats probationary and trial-period employees 
  1900  outside the retention-register process and permits agencies to retain, 
  1901  finalize, or separate them under the rules applicable to their 
  1902  appointments, instead of the RIF rules.
  1903      Further, the modal-rating approach does not address the separate 
  1904  legal and personnel-management function of probationary and trial 
  1905  periods. Civil Service Rule 11 provides that agencies must use 
  1906  probationary and trial periods to evaluate an employee's fitness and 
  1907  whether continued employment advances the public interest; the agency 
  1908  may consider performance and conduct, agency needs, organizational 
  1909  goals, and efficiency of the service before finalizing the appointment. 
  1910  A modal RIF rating cannot replace that appointment-finalization 
  1911  judgment. It does not tell the agency whether the employee has 
  1912  demonstrated sufficient fitness, adaptability, conduct, judgment, or 
  1913  mission fit to warrant final appointment. It simply imputes a rating 
  1914  based on how other employees were rated. That is a poor fit for 
  1915  employees who are still in the government's final assessment period.
  1916      Commenters 0674 and 0680 argued that excluding temporary, 
  1917  probationary and trial period employees from RIF procedures could mean 
  1918  that certain employees still covered by RIF regulations would be 
  1919  released ahead of more junior employees, thus undermining tenure as a 
  1920  statutory retention factor. But 5 U.S.C. 3502 does not prescribe a 
  1921  strict ``last in, first out'' system. It does not define ``competing 
  1922  employees,'' does not require every employee in an agency to compete 
  1923  against every other employee, and does not require agencies to retain 
  1924  every more senior employee ahead of every less senior employee in all 
  1925  circumstances. Instead, it directed OPM to create regulations for the 
  1926  release of competing employees and to give ``due effect'' to several 
  1927  factors. ``Due effect'' does not mean controlling effect, equal effect, 
  1928  or absolute effect in every possible comparison. Nor does it mean that 
  1929  tenure must always override appointment status, performance, agency 
  1930  needs, or the threshold question whether an employee has a finalized 
  1931  appointment and belongs in RIF competition at all. OPM therefore may 
  1932  reasonably distinguish between employees who have completed the period 
  1933  necessary to obtain a finalized appointment and employees who remain in 
  1934  a temporary, probationary, or trial status.
  1935      Commenter 0115 expressed concern that excluding probationary and 
  1936  temporary employees from RIF procedures might hurt efforts to recruit 
  1937  early-career talent. However, probationary, trial period, and temporary 
  1938  employees are the most likely to be separated under the current RIF 
  1939  rules, which require agencies to place these employees at the bottom of

[2026-15665: lines 2060-2254 of 6220, FR page 49194]
  2060      This rule modifies the current definitions in Sec.  351.203 for 
  2061  current rating of record and rating of record. The revision to current 
  2062  rating of record updates the cross reference within part 351. The 
  2063  revision to rating of record clarifies that only the annual performance 
  2064  evaluation--and not a mid-year within-grade evaluation--can be used 
  2065  when computing the performance credit, which is used for determining 
  2066  standing on the retention register. OPM did not receive significant 
  2067  adverse comment regarding these changes.
  2068      OPM is also adding meanings for agency, Government obligation and 
  2069  military spouse, and to correct a typo in Sec.  351.204 to change 
  2070  ``reduction force'' to ``reduction in force.'' OPM did not receive 
  2071  significant adverse comment regarding these proposed changes. As 
  2072  discussed further below, OPM is also adding a definition for 
  2073  restoration protected employee.
  2074      Commenter 0687 suggested that OPM add an anti-manipulation 
  2075  provision to state clearly that agencies may not manipulate competitive 
  2076  areas to purposefully target employees in ways
  2077  
  2078  [[Page 49195]]
  2079  
  2080  that are inconsistent with Merit System Principles. OPM agrees, in 
  2081  part, and is adding a provision to Sec.  351.204, setting forth the 
  2082  responsibilities of agencies, to clarify that agencies are not only 
  2083  responsible for following and applying the RIF regulations, but for 
  2084  ensuring that such regulations are administered and applied consistent 
  2085  with the Merit System Principles set forth in 5 U.S.C. 2301(b). OPM

  3395  IV. Implementation Considerations
  3396  
  3397      OPM recognizes that agencies that may be conducting RIFs may be 
  3398  impacted by the changes resulting from this rule, particularly where an 
  3399  agency has recently issued RIF notices with RIF effective dates that 
  3400  may occur near the effective date of this rule. To provide clear

  3402  final

  3406  rule based on the date the agency issues the RIF notice.
  3407      An agency that issues a RIF notice before September 2, 2026 must 
  3408  process the RIF under the regulations in effect when the notice was 
  3409  issued. An agency that issues a RIF notice on or after September 2, 
  3410  2026 must apply the RIF provisions as amended by this final rule. OPM 
  3411  believes that this implementation approach provides clear and 
  3412  consistent guidance to agencies. It also aligns with the revised 
  3413  regulations, under which the effective date of retention standing is 
  3414  calculated as of the date the employee receives the RIF notice, rather 
  3415  than the RIF effective date (typically 60 days after issuance of the 
  3416  RIF notice).
  3417  
  3418  V. Expected Impact of This Rule
  3419  
  3420  A. Statement of Need
  3421  
  3422      OPM is finalizing these revisions because the existing RIF 
  3423  regulations no longer provide agencies, employees, or the public with a 
  3424  sufficiently clear, efficient, flexible, and merit-based framework for 
  3425  managing workforce reductions and organizational realignments. RIF 
  3426  rules determine not only which positions are abolished, but which 
  3427  employees remain to carry out the Government's continuing 
  3428  responsibilities after a reduction. The public interest is therefore 
  3429  not served by a system that treats RIFs as a mechanical exercise in 
  3430  tenure-based ordering, rather than as a workforce-shaping process that 
  3431  seeks to preserve agency capacity, operational continuity, and the 
  3432  ability to perform mission-critical work.
  3433      The statutory RIF framework directs OPM to prescribe regulations 
  3434  giving due effect to tenure of employment, military preference, length 
  3435  of service, and efficiency or performance ratings. The statute does not 
  3436  require OPM to preserve the current regulatory hierarchy or to 
  3437  subordinate performance to tenure and length of service. OPM has 
  3438  concluded that the current rules do not give sufficiently meaningful 
  3439  effect to performance and are not adequately suited to the needs of 
  3440  modern agencies. Under current regulations, employees are ranked first 
  3441  by tenure, then veterans' preference, then length of service, with 
  3442  performance used only to augment service credit; as OPM explained in 
  3443  the proposed rule, this structure may result in higher-performing 
  3444  employees being separated while lower-performing, more senior employees 
  3445  are retained.
  3446      Several commenters agreed that the existing RIF system has become 
  3447  too complex, too burdensome, and insufficiently aligned with agency 
  3448  mission needs. Commenter 0685 explained that RIF policy directly 
  3449  affects agency effectiveness by influencing which employees are 
  3450  retained, how quickly restructuring can occur, and how resources are 
  3451  allocated across mission-critical functions; it further observed that 
  3452  current rules have accumulated layers of procedural requirements and 
  3453  categorical distinctions that can impede timely workforce adjustments. 
  3454  Commenter 0720, a Federal agency, similarly described its current RIF 
  3455  process as requiring complex tenure groupings, broad competitive-area 
  3456  analyses, manual retention registers, bump-and-retreat determinations, 
  3457  transfer-of-function analyses, and coordination with CTAP, ICTAP, and 
  3458  RPL, all of which impose substantial operational burdens.
  3459      The Federal Government's missions have changed substantially since 
  3460  the current RIF framework was developed. Agencies now operate in 
  3461  environments shaped by evolving statutory responsibilities, constrained 
  3462  budgets, changing technology, new skill requirements, diverse hiring 
  3463  authorities, distributed worksites, and complex organizational 
  3464  structures. Commenter 0687 emphasized that agencies need tools to 
  3465  right-size and realign their workforces in response to labor-market 
  3466  disruption, advances in technology, and congressionally directed 
  3467  mission changes, and that personnel systems must be flexible enough to 
  3468  ensure agencies have the right people, with the right skills, for the 
  3469  missions assigned to them. Commenter 0719, a Federal agency, likewise 
  3470  explained that changing mission needs, budget environments, evolving 
  3471  skill requirements, varied hiring and funding structures, and 
  3472  administrative barriers under current rules can hinder operational 
  3473  agility and effective service to the public.
  3474      The current rules also impose real administrative costs. OPM 
  3475  explained in the proposed rule that a RIF can be a complex operational 
  3476  endeavor that may take as long as 14 months from planning through 
  3477  completion, with time-consuming tasks including review of position 
  3478  descriptions, validation of competitive levels, verification of 
  3479  veterans' preference and service computation dates, updating 
  3480  qualifications data, and creation of retention registers. For example, 
  3481  Commenter 0720, a Federal agency, reported a large and heterogeneous 
  3482  workforce across multiple appointment types, probationary categories, 
  3483  special hiring authorities, and retention right classifications, and 
  3484  explained that manual processes for retention registers and transition 
  3485  programs can become unsustainable when affected populations exceed 200 
  3486  employees.
  3487      OPM is also finalizing this rule because retaining high performers 
  3488  during a RIF is essential to effective government. A RIF leaves an 
  3489  agency with fewer employees to perform continuing work. The employees 
  3490  who remain must maintain operations, absorb mission-critical 
  3491  responsibilities, implement new priorities, and preserve public service 
  3492  delivery. Commenter 0673 opined that performance has been 
  3493  systematically underweighted in current RIF competition and that the 
  3494  proposed rule better links retention to efficiency, performance, and 
  3495  contribution to agency mission success. Commenter 0720 similarly stated 
  3496  that when RIFs are necessary, agency operations benefit from retaining 
  3497  the highest-performing and most effective employees, and that 
  3498  performance ratings are a more direct measure of contribution than pure 
  3499  seniority.
  3500      The final rule addresses this need by replacing the current 
  3501  performance-adjusted service computation date model with a more 
  3502  transparent performance-credit model. Performance will be measured 
  3503  directly through numerical credit for ratings of record, veterans' 
  3504  preference will be added as explicit additional credit, tenure subgroup 
  3505  will resolve ties, and actual service computation date will resolve 
  3506  remaining ties. This approach gives effect to each statutory factor 
  3507  while making the retention register easier to understand, administer, 
  3508  and audit. OPM's final rule provides that employees will be ranked by 
  3509  tenure group, then by performance credit as augmented by veterans' 
  3510  preference, and then--where scores are tied--by tenure subgroup and 
  3511  service computation date.
  3512      OPM also agrees with commenters that modernization must preserve 
  3513  structure and predictability. This rule is not intended to replace 
  3514  clear rules with unbounded discretion. Rather, it establishes a more 
  3515  coherent framework: ratings of record are used under defined lookback 
  3516  rules; agencies may establish cutoff dates; performance credit must be 
  3517  applied uniformly and consistently within the competitive area; 
  3518  veterans' preference remains a substantial component of retention 
  3519  standing; tenure and length of service remain part of the ranking 
  3520  process; and employees continue to receive notice and access to 
  3521  pertinent records. These guardrails respond to commenters who supported 
  3522  greater flexibility and performance-based retention while emphasizing 
  3523  the importance of clarity, documentation, and consistent application.
  3524  
  3525  [[Page 49208]]
  3526  
  3527      This rule also addresses the need to preserve workforce pipelines 
  3528  and future agency capacity. Current rules can require agencies to 
  3529  release the least-tenured employees first, even where those employees 
  3530  represent high-potential early-career talent in which the agency has

**Identifying regulatory inconsistencies**

I’m comparing the preamble’s explanations with the operative regulatory text and have found a significant mismatch: one passage says the retention-standing date is when the employee receives the reduction-in-force notice, while another says it is when the notice is issued. The regulation uses the receipt date.

I’m also noting a citation error concerning transfer-function losers. The preamble refers to §351.302(b), but the final regulatory text places the relevant adverse-action procedure in §351.302(d). These inconsistencies should be listed and checked against the other cited sections.**Comparing paragraph details**

I’m confirming one clear mismatch: the preamble describes §351.602 as removing only a prohibition on temporary appointments, whereas the operative text covers both temporary and term promotions.

The other points appear consistent so far. The discussion of dates, restoration or reemployment, agency cutoff periods, reassignment within an abolished competitive area, and post-restoration protection generally matches the regulatory language. I’m still checking the service-length thresholds, because the preamble’s wording—one year after more than 180 days and six months after service exceeding 30 days—needs to align precisely with the final text.

**Reviewing regulatory language**

I’m checking whether the preamble accurately reflects the cited regulation. The retention period appears to be six months or one year, and the relevant provision is §353.209(b), rather than a reprint citation. The preamble’s reference to 180 days is consistent with six months.

I’m also confirming that USERRA retention and restoration protections operate as mandatory exceptions when another competing employee could otherwise be released. If an entire competitive area is abolished and no competing employee may be released, the agency cannot separate the protected employee and must instead assign them as required.**Comparing regulatory provisions**

I’m checking several wording differences between the preamble and the regulatory text. References to agency abolition, assistance, sick leave, and retirement or health-benefits coverage appear substantively consistent, though some phrasing is less precise. The examples involving five-year lookback periods and recent performance ratings also match the stated regulatory periods.

I’m noticing a minor ambiguity where the preamble refers to the “date of the RIF notice,” while another provision says when the employee “receives” notice. Because that distinction isn’t clearly substantive here, I’m not treating it as a definitive discrepancy.

**Reviewing regulatory details**

I’m checking each statement against the cited provisions and distinguishing the final rule from its preamble. For §351.802(a)(2), the wording concerns an employee’s three most recent ratings received during the previous four years. The claims about §351.604 appear accurate because the preamble discusses furlough decisions based on retention standing without changing the regulatory text. Likewise, §351.605 includes positions otherwise excluded under §351.202(d), requires abolition within 180 days, and does not require agencies to rank employees. I’m still verifying the §351.204 reference.**Comparing regulatory language**

I’m checking the proposed explanations against the final text, focusing on whether differences are substantive or merely labeling issues. The §351.302(b) discrepancy appears significant, while references to §351.302(c) and (d) may simply misidentify the applicable subsections. For §351.402(c), the explanation seems broadly accurate but may omit the provision covering materially modified competitive areas. Regarding §351.503(d) and (e), the discussion of additional performance credit appears consistent with the regulation, including exceptional performance, awards, and the highest performance pattern requirement.

**Identifying a regulatory mismatch**

I’m comparing the preamble’s explanation with the text of §351.503(e)(1)(i). The preamble says agencies may use documented evidence consistent with the criteria in revised §351.503(d), whose first category includes special-act or service awards. However, §351.503(e)(1)(i) appears narrower: it mentions only the highest agency or departmental award, a QSI, or appraisal awards or bonuses. That creates a possible inconsistency between the preamble’s broad reference to subsection (d) and the regulation’s more limited list.**Checking related provisions**

I’m treating the awards issue as a potential mismatch rather than assuming the preamble incorporates every criterion from subsection (d). The operative text in subsection (e)(1) expressly omits special-act or service awards, while the preamble refers broadly to subsection (d)’s criteria; I haven’t identified a separate passage correcting or clarifying that difference.

The other provisions I’m reviewing appear consistent: the discussion of summary patterns and prior systems matches the regulatory cross-references, the discretion to credit performance above Level 3 is accurately described, and the preference-point values are correctly stated.

**Comparing regulatory statements**

I’m checking whether the preamble accurately reflects the referenced provisions. The subgroup classification under AD/A/B appears to be stated correctly, and the preamble’s discussion of complete records under §351.506 also matches the provision.

For §351.701, I’m noticing a potentially meaningful omission: the sec­tion-by-section discussion describes assignment rights within three grades below the prior position but does not mention the five-grade exception for certain preference-eligible employees with qualifying disabilities. Elsewhere, the preamble includes that exception, so the inconsistency may be limited to that specific discussion.**Assessing substantive differences**

I’m including the §351.701 sentence because it states the three-grade limit without the applicable five-grade exception, while the executive summary correctly describes the rule as generally three grades and five for qualifying disabled employees. The same-tenure-group assignment context matches the regulation, as does the explanation that Level 2 performance ratings no longer restrict selection.

For §351.702, I’m identifying a possible wording difference: the preamble appears to prohibit reliance on automated self-assessment altogether, while the regulation prohibits relying on it solely or principally. That may overstate the final rule.

**Comparing regulatory language**

I’m checking whether the preamble accurately reflects the operative provisions. One mismatch appears in its description of an assessment: the regulatory text says it must not consist solely or principally of an automated self-assessment, while the preamble uses different wording that may be less precise. The preamble’s statement about validated assessments reducing subjectivity also seems incomplete.

The §351.702(d) exception appears accurately described. However, I’m uncertain whether the discussion of §351.705 correctly explains the renumbering and amendment of its paragraphs.**Verifying possible mismatches**

I’m finding that the §351.705 renumbering may not be a mismatch after all; the current paragraph (c) appears to become paragraph (a). Several other areas remain stronger candidates for discrepancies:

- §351.302(d) may cite the wrong paragraph.
- §351.507 appears to confuse issuance with receipt.
- Performance-pattern criteria may differ between §351.503(d) and (e).
- A three-grade assignment limitation may omit a preference-eligible exception.
- Assessment language may not precisely track the regulation.
- §351.608(d) may overstate how other leave relates to sick leave.

**Reviewing retention rules**

I’m examining how restoration protections interact with a reduction in force. The key point appears to be that a protected employee may need to be assigned to another position rather than separated, but only when no other competing employee can be released—for example, when an entire organizational area is abolished.

I’m also checking the provision addressing agency-wide abolitions and situations where reassignment is impossible or unreasonable, since those circumstances may trigger assistance. One citation or paragraph reference may not align, so I’m verifying that section carefully.**Checking preamble consistency**

I’m comparing the explanatory preamble with the regulatory text and separating genuine discrepancies from statements clarified elsewhere. The notice requirement appears accurate: affected employees must receive written notice under the referenced provision, and the preamble’s discussion of reemployment rights likely corresponds to the stated notice contents.

I’m identifying a clearer inconsistency about whether the relevant date is when notice is issued or received. I’m also flagging an apparently overbroad statement about grade intervals and a narrower regulatory standard concerning examination methods. Each issue should be listed once, with page references and any correcting passage noted.

**Comparing regulatory language**

I’m checking whether the preamble and amended text express the same intent. The apparent discrepancy may be only a phrasing issue, so I’m avoiding an overstatement and describing the preamble as sounding absolute while the regulatory language permits limited non-principal use.

For §351.201, I’m seeing a clearer mismatch: the preamble attributes a change to §351.201(a)(2), but the relevant amendment appears in §351.202(c)(3). The preamble first describes removing an existing trigger, then discusses a new prohibition, while the final text leaves §351.201(a)(2) unchanged.**Checking section references**

I’m finding a strong discrepancy in the discussion of §351.201(a)(2): the preamble says it is being modified to remove an erosion-related trigger, but that provision remains unchanged in the final text. The operative amendment instead appears in §351.202(c)(3), which establishes a different timing-based prohibition affecting standing during a reduction in force. I’m also noting possible citation mismatches for the transfer-function provision and temporary-assignment rights, plus a “notice issued” versus “notice received” inconsistency. Other points appear accurate or outside the requested comparison.

**Reconciling regulatory details**

summary.text:
**Comparing appeal provisions**

I’m focusing only on Question 14 and have enough information to proceed. The preamble and final text appear consistent on the main points: appeal rights apply when an employee is furloughed for more than 30 days, separated, or demoted, including actions taken under part 351. The preamble also accurately states that an appeal must be submitted within 30 calendar days, with the deadline occurring at 11:59 p.m.**Checking final-rule consistency**

I’m comparing the preamble with the final regulatory text. Most points match: appeals are the exclusive route for RIF actions, related matters cannot proceed through grievance procedures, judicial review remains unavailable, hearings are discretionary, and agencies must provide the required record and notice information.

The main issue I’m checking is whether the preamble overstates public availability of final decisions. The text appears narrower, covering decisions addressing merits claims while limiting access in some circumstances. I’m also noting the corrected deadline language: 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time, not Eastern Standard Time.

**Comparing rule and preamble**

I’m identifying a direct tension between the operative text and its preamble. The preamble says the rule does not retroactively invalidate existing collective-bargaining agreements, while §351.901(c)(2) appears to bar negotiated grievances or arbitration for the covered reduction-in-force action and related appeals, regardless of an existing agreement.

The text contains no clear grandfather clause, and the two statements aren’t expressly reconciled. I’ll present this as a significant inconsistency between the regulation’s categorical language and the preamble’s assurance about existing agreements.**Checking preamble consistency**

I’m finding that several preamble explanations closely track the regulatory text: limits on judicial review, exclusion of grievance and collateral claims, tolling provisions, finality timelines, and the standard for correcting material factual errors.

I’m still checking for a clearer discrepancy, including possible section-reference errors or differences in how appeal deadlines and initial decisions are described. The strongest previously identified issue remains the tension concerning collective-bargaining agreements, while these other examples appear substantially consistent with the operative provisions.

  2279  IV. Section-by-Section Analysis
  2280  
  2281      In this section, OPM discusses the regulatory amendments to 5 CFR 
  2282  chapter I, subchapter B, part 351, subpart I, governing appeals of and 
  2283  corrective action with respect to RIFs.
  2284  
  2285  A. Section 351.802--Content of Notice
  2286  
  2287      OPM is revising Sec.  351.802(a)(6), which governs the information 
  2288  an agency must include in a written notice to an employee affected by a 
  2289  reduction in force. Current Sec.  351.802(a)(6) refers to the 
  2290  employee's right to appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board. 
  2291  Because this final rule transfers adjudication of covered RIF appeals 
  2292  from MSPB to OPM, revised Sec.  351.802(a)(6) replaces the MSPB 
  2293  reference with a reference to OPM.
  2294      The revised provision requires an agency's RIF notice to inform the 
  2295  employee, as applicable, of the employee's right to appeal to OPM. As 
  2296  revised in this final rule, the notice must also state the time limit 
  2297  for filing an appeal under Sec.  351.902(b) and identify the electronic 
  2298  filing system, available on OPM's website, through which an appeal must 
  2299  be filed. This requirement preserves the practical filing information 
  2300  previously conveyed through the cross-reference to Sec.  1201.21 of 
  2301  this title and forecloses any contention that a RIF notice failed to 
  2302  apprise an employee of how and when to appeal. The provision is 
  2303  conforming in nature and is intended to ensure that employees receive 
  2304  accurate notice of the administrative appeal forum established by 
  2305  revised subpart I. The revision does not eliminate any independently 
  2306  applicable statutory notice requirement or any separately available 
  2307  remedial process administered by another entity.
  2308      The proposed rule retained legacy language in Sec.  351.802(a)(6) 
  2309  requiring agencies to comply with Sec.  1201.21 of this title, as 
  2310  applicable. OPM is removing that cross-reference in the final rule. 
  2311  Section 1201.21 is an MSPB notice provision that applies when an agency 
  2312  issues a decision notice in a matter appealable to the Board. It 
  2313  requires MSPB-specific information, including notice of the time limits 
  2314  for appealing to the Board, the address of the appropriate Board 
  2315  office, access to the Board's regulations, and access to the MSPB 
  2316  appeal form. Because this final rule replaces MSPB with OPM as the 
  2317  adjudicative forum for RIF appeals under part 351, retaining an 
  2318  unqualified cross-reference to Sec.  1201.21 in the RIF notice 
  2319  provision could create confusion about where an affected employee must 
  2320  file a RIF appeal.

  2337      OPM is revising Sec.  351.807(e), which concerns agency

  2339  The prior provision referred to appeal to MSPB. Revised Sec.  
  2340  351.807(e) removes that MSPB reference and states that an agency

  2342      This change is also conforming in nature. It aligns Sec.  
  2343  351.807(e) with revised subpart I and clarifies that certification 
  2344  determinations under Sec.  351.807 are not independently appealable 
  2345  under part 351. Employees who are actually furloughed for more than 30

  2349  C. Subpart I--Appeals
  2350  
  2351      OPM is revising subpart I of part 351 in full. Revised subpart I 
  2352  establishes the procedures governing appeals to OPM by employees who 
  2353  are subject to covered RIF actions. The revised subpart identifies who 
  2354  may appeal, the burden of proof, filing requirements, party 
  2355  submissions, representation rules, adjudication procedures, remedies, 
  2356  sanctions, reconsideration, Director review, and finality.
  2357  1. Section 351.901--Right To Appeal
  2358      Revised Sec.  351.901 establishes the right to appeal a covered 
  2359  reduction-in-force action to OPM, identifies the appellant's burden of 
  2360  proof, and defines the relationship between the OPM RIF appeal process 
  2361  and other remedial forums.
  2362      Paragraph (a) provides that an employee who has been furloughed for 
  2363  more than 30 days, separated, or demoted by a reduction-in-force action 
  2364  taken under part 351 may appeal that action to OPM. This paragraph 
  2365  identifies the covered actions that may be appealed under subpart I and 
  2366  implements the rule's central procedural change: OPM, rather than MSPB, 
  2367  will adjudicate appeals of covered RIF actions, subject to the 
  2368  applicability provision described below.
  2369      Paragraph (b) establishes the employee's burden of proof. The 
  2370  appellant must prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the 
  2371  written appeal was timely and in the required form; that OPM has 
  2372  jurisdiction over the appeal; that the agency failed to comply with an 
  2373  applicable statute or OPM regulation governing reduction-in-force 
  2374  actions under part 351; and that the failure prejudiced the appellant.
  2375      Paragraph (b)(4) defines the prejudice requirement. The appellant 
  2376  must show that the agency's failure to comply with an applicable RIF 
  2377  statute or OPM regulation caused the appellant to be subjected to the 
  2378  appealed action or to lose a materially more favorable outcome under 
  2379  part 351. This standard is intended to distinguish prejudicial errors 
  2380  from technical or immaterial errors. OPM will not grant relief solely 
  2381  because an agency committed a procedural or technical error if the 
  2382  appellant would have been subject to the same action, or would not have 
  2383  received a materially more favorable outcome, had the agency complied 
  2384  with the applicable requirement. Conversely, prejudice may exist where 
  2385  the violation affected the appellant's retention standing, order of 
  2386  release, assignment rights, notice rights, or other RIF determination 
  2387  in a way that materially affected the outcome of the RIF action as 
  2388  applied to the appellant.
  2389      Paragraph (c)(1) provides that the procedures in part 351 are the 
  2390  sole and exclusive means of appealing a RIF action covered by this 
  2391  subpart. This provision is intended to avoid duplicative or overlapping 
  2392  RIF appeal processes and to channel covered RIF appeals through the OPM 
  2393  procedure established by this final rule. It also promotes consistent 
  2394  application of OPM's governmentwide RIF regulations and avoids parallel 
  2395  adjudication of the same RIF-compliance issues in multiple forums.
  2396      Paragraph (c)(2) provides that a reduction-in-force action taken 
  2397  under part 351, and any matter relating to an appeal of such an action, 
  2398  may not be raised under a negotiated grievance procedure or contested 
  2399  through grievance arbitration. This provision forecloses negotiated 
  2400  grievance procedures and grievance arbitration as alternative forums 
  2401  for direct RIF-compliance challenges, for the reasons discussed in 
  2402  Section III.I of this preamble.
  2403      At the same time, paragraph (c)(3) makes clear that the OPM RIF 
  2404  appeal process does not displace matters within the independent 
  2405  jurisdiction of other entities. Employees may continue to file 
  2406  complaints, appeals, or other matters that fall within the independent 
  2407  jurisdiction of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, an 
  2408  Inspector General, MSPB, the Department of Labor Veterans' Employment 
  2409  and Training Service, or the Office of Special Counsel. Thus, OPM will 
  2410  adjudicate whether the RIF action complied with applicable RIF statutes 
  2411  and OPM regulations, while collateral statutory claims remain available 
  2412  in the forums Congress or applicable law has designated for those 
  2413  claims.
  2414      Paragraph (c)(4) also provides that a party cannot obtain judicial 
  2415  review of a decision under this subpart. OPM addresses comments 
  2416  concerning judicial review and the CSRA remedial scheme in Section 
  2417  III.G.
  2418      Consistent with the DATES section of this preamble, the appeal 
  2419  process established by revised Sec.  351.901 and subpart I is available 
  2420  for a reduction-in-force action for which the agency issued the 
  2421  employee a specific RIF notice under Sec.  351.802 on or after the 
  2422  effective date of the final rule under RIN 3206-AO86. An appeal of a 
  2423  reduction-in-force action for which the agency issued that notice 
  2424  before that date--including an appeal pending before the MSPB--

summary.text:
**Comparing preamble and regulation**

I’m evaluating whether the preamble and regulatory text conflict. The appeal-eligibility statement appears to be a preamble explanation tied to the effective date, while §351.901(a) does not independently address applicability, so I’m not treating that as a mismatch.

The closer issue is §351.903(e). The preamble describes service as subject to paragraph (b)’s disclosure limitations, but the regulatory text instead lists separate limits, including privacy restrictions, privileges, classified information, and protective orders. I’m flagging that wording as potentially imprecise rather than assuming the provisions align perfectly.**Reviewing cross-references**

I’m treating the paragraph (e) discussion as a likely preamble mismatch: it points to paragraph (b)’s disclosure limits, while paragraph (e) contains its own separate exceptions. The section analysis for paragraph (d) also appears incomplete because it omits applicable legal privileges and possibly other stated limits.

The remaining provisions I’m checking appear consistent with the regulatory text, including adjudicator restrictions, requests for additional information, and protective-order limits. For final decisions, I’m noting that the preamble’s description of availability may be broader than the text’s narrower access conditions.

**Verifying regulatory interpretations**

I’m checking which statements are supported exactly by the cited provisions and which go beyond the regulatory text. The preamble appears to state that §351.904(b) concerns neither duty status nor reimbursement. It also says §351.901(c) excludes RIF and appeal-related issues from grievances, though that may conflict with collective-bargaining provisions.

For §351.902(b)(3), I’m confirming the 30-day filing period after a materially affecting final decision and the description of rating-correction complaints. I’m also distinguishing §351.903(a)’s form requirements from §351.901(b)’s express timeliness requirement.**Comparing textual support**

I’m separating statements that match the regulation from interpretations that may be broader. The burden provision expressly lists timeliness, jurisdiction, noncompliance, and prejudice; it does not separately say the employee must prove compliance with every formatting requirement, even though the appeal itself must be written.

I’m also confirming that the §351.903(c) preamble permits new error allegations only when based on newly disclosed information or good cause. The hearing statement under §351.905(c) appears supported. For §351.909(f), I’m distinguishing the text’s limits on posted merits decisions from broader preamble language.
