summary.text:
**Comparing regulatory language**

I’m identifying inconsistencies between the preamble and regulatory text. One passage references service limits in §351.903(b), while the text describes the provision as independent, so I’m noting that discrepancy.

The strongest issue concerns §351.901(c)(2): although the preamble says the rule won’t retroactively invalidate existing collective bargaining agreements, the regulatory text appears to bar raising covered reduction-in-force actions or related matters through negotiated grievances, without an effective-date or transition exception.

I’m also comparing “covered RIF action” in the preamble with the broader wording “a RIF action taken under part 351” in §351.901(c)(1).**Assessing applicability differences**

I’m focusing on a likely mismatch involving effective dates. The preamble states that the rule applies only to reduction-in-force notices issued on or after September 2, while §351.901 itself does not contain an equivalent applicability limitation.

The preamble reportedly acknowledges that the regulatory text omits a separate applicability provision, making this a meaningful difference between the explanatory discussion and the published rule. I’m also checking whether references to appeal rights for employees furloughed more than 30 days, separated, or demoted create additional scope differences, though that issue may be less central.

**Comparing applicability language**

I’m identifying a direct discrepancy between the preamble and the regulatory text. **Comparing jurisdiction rules**

I’m identifying two internal inconsistencies in the Board’s discussion. First, one section says appeals are accepted when the agency’s RIF notice was issued before the relevant date, while another limits post-date appeals to cases whose RIF effective date preceded September 2. That creates uncertainty when notice came earlier but the effective date came later. Second, the regulatory text removes non–Foreign Service RIF jurisdiction without a transition clause, even though the preamble appears to preserve certain existing cases. The dates section is also less precise than the surrounding language.**Reconciling transition rules**

I’m separating two related conflicts. First, the Board uses different transition triggers: its opening dates statement refers broadly to agency actions before September 2, another passage refers to RIF effective dates before September 2, and a further passage uses the notice-issuance date. Second, the regulatory text preserves only Foreign Service RIF jurisdiction, while the preamble appears to preserve pending or legacy non–Foreign Service appeals. The OPM transition rule also relies on notice timing, creating a direct mismatch when notice and effective dates fall on opposite sides of September 2.

**Clarifying effective dates**

I’m examining a discrepancy between the OPM rule and the Board’s wording about legacy MSPB procedures after September 2. The key issue is whether applicability depends on the notice date or the effective date; a notice issued after September 2 with an earlier effective date seems impossible unless retroactivity is involved.

I’m also checking the cross-reference in §351.903(e), the relevant preamble language, and the revised provisions replacing prior regulations. The furlough discussion appears to reference revised §351.901, though it doesn’t clearly explain how pre-September 2 RIF notices are treated.**Checking regulatory wording**

I’m comparing the preamble with the final regulatory text, especially where the preamble describes §351.901(b)(1) as requiring both a timely appeal and a particular form. The regulation itself appears to address timeliness but may not expressly include the form requirement, so I’m deciding whether that discrepancy should be noted directly.

I’m also reviewing the discussion of §351.902 and reconsideration of an initial decision, checking whether the preamble’s paragraph references accurately match the final provisions.

  2798  appropriate part of the noncompliant party's filings or submissions.
  2799      OPM is additionally specifying in paragraph (c) that any sanction 
  2800  issued under paragraph (b) must be proportionate, causally related to 
  2801  the violation, and no broader than necessary to protect the 
  2802  adjudicatory process.
  2803  
  2804  [[Page 49252]]
  2805  
  2806  7. Section 351.907--Reconsideration of an Initial Decision
  2807      Revised Sec.  351.907 establishes the process for reconsideration 
  2808  of an initial decision.
  2809      Paragraph (a) authorizes OPM, in its sole discretion, to reopen and 
  2810  reconsider an initial decision upon request of either party or on OPM's 
  2811  own initiative. An employee, the employee's representative, or the 
  2812  agency may request reconsideration within 30 calendar days from 
  2813  issuance of the initial decision. The request must be filed in the same 
  2814  manner as an initial appeal.
  2815      Paragraph (b) identifies the grounds on which OPM may grant 
  2816  reconsideration. OPM may grant reconsideration if the initial decision 
  2817  contains erroneous findings of material fact sufficient to warrant a 
  2818  different outcome; if the initial decision is based on an erroneous 
  2819  interpretation of statute or regulation or an erroneous application of 
  2820  law to the facts; if new and material evidence or legal argument is 
  2821  available that, despite the party's due diligence, was not available 
  2822  when the record closed; or if OPM finds good cause to reconsider the 
  2823  appeal.
  2824      When a party alleges legal error, the party must explain how the 
  2825  error affected the outcome of the case. For new evidence, the relevant 
  2826  question is whether the information contained in the documents, not 
  2827  merely the documents themselves, was unavailable despite due diligence 
  2828  when the record closed.
  2829      Paragraph (c) describes OPM's authority in a reopened or reviewed 
  2830  case. OPM may issue a reopened and reconsidered decision that affirms, 
  2831  reverses, modifies, vacates, or otherwise decides the case in whole or 
  2832  in part. OPM may require the parties to submit argument and evidence, 
  2833  take any other action necessary for final disposition of the case, and 
  2834  issue an order with a date for compliance.
  2835      Paragraph (d) provides that there is no further right of 
  2836  administrative appeal from the reopened and reconsidered decision.
  2837  8. Section 351.908--Review by the OPM Director
  2838      Section 351.908 reserves to the OPM Director the authority, in the 
  2839  Director's discretion and sua sponte, to reopen and reconsider any 
  2840  appeal in which OPM has issued a decision that has not yet become 
  2841  final. Once a decision becomes final under Sec.  351.909, Sec.  351.908 
  2842  does not provide a separate mechanism for reopening that decision.
  2843      Many commenters (including 0177, 0395, 0411, 0555, 1020, and 
  2844  others) objected to providing the OPM Director with the authority to 
  2845  reopen and reconsider decisions at his or her direction, sua sponte, 
  2846  contending that it violated due process.
  2847      In response to comments expressing concern that Director review 
  2848  could be too open-ended or could undermine the perceived neutrality of 
  2849  OPM adjudication, OPM has revised Sec.  351.908 to identify 
  2850  nonexclusive considerations that may inform the Director's decision to 
  2851  reopen and reconsider a nonfinal RIF appeal decision. Under the final 
  2852  rule, the Director may act on the Director's own initiative and only 
  2853  before a decision becomes final under Sec.  351.909. In determining 
  2854  whether to exercise that authority, the Director may consider, among 
  2855  other things, whether the decision contains clear legal error, rests on 
  2856  an erroneous finding of material fact, involves an issue of exceptional 
  2857  importance, affects the governmentwide administration of civil service 
  2858  laws, rules, regulations, or OPM policy, conflicts with another OPM 
  2859  decision, or otherwise warrants Director review.
  2860      This revision responds to commenters who objected to Director 
  2861  review as insufficiently cabined, while preserving final agency 
  2862  supervision over important legal, factual, policy, consistency, and 
  2863  governmentwide civil service issues. OPM has retained sua sponte 
  2864  Director review because final agency oversight promotes decisional 
  2865  consistency and accountability within OPM's adjudicatory process. The 
  2866  revision does not create a separate right for parties to request 
  2867  Director review; parties may seek reconsideration under Sec.  351.907. 
  2868  If the Director reopens and reconsiders a decision under Sec.  351.908, 
  2869  the Director may take any action available under Sec.  351.907(c). This 
  2870  structure preserves meaningful principal-officer oversight while 
  2871  clarifying that Director review will occur within the rule's record-
  2872  based adjudicatory framework, including the final rule's agency-record, 
  2873  separation-of-functions, ex parte, reconsideration, and finality 
  2874  provisions.
  2875      OPM declines to eliminate Director review entirely. Director review 
  2876  serves both administrative and constitutional functions. As an 
  2877  administrative matter, it ensures that OPM can correct material legal, 
  2878  factual, or procedural errors before a decision becomes final; resolve 
  2879  recurring or important questions of interpretation; and promote uniform 
  2880  application of part 351 across agencies. That review function is 
  2881  especially important in a governmentwide personnel system, where 
  2882  inconsistent interpretations by subordinate adjudicators could produce 
  2883  uneven appeal rights for similarly situated employees in different 
  2884  agencies. Cf. 5 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1), (3), (5) (vesting the OPM Director 
  2885  with responsibility for securing ``accuracy, uniformity, and justice'' 
  2886  in OPM's functions, directing and supervising OPM employees, and 
  2887  executing, administering, and enforcing civil-service laws and 
  2888  regulations).
  2889      Director review also reinforces the rule's consistency with the 
  2890  Appointments Clause. The Constitution requires principal officers to be 
  2891  appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, 
  2892  while Congress may vest appointment of inferior officers in the 
  2893  President alone, courts of law, or heads of departments. U.S. Const. 
  2894  art. II, Sec.  2, cl. 2. The OPM Director is a presidentially 
  2895  appointed, Senate-confirmed officer. 5 U.S.C. 1102(a). Under the 
  2896  Supreme Court's Appointments Clause precedents, inferior officers must 
  2897  remain subject to direction and supervision by a properly appointed 
  2898  superior officer. Edmond v. United States, 520 U.S. 651, 663-65 (1997). 
  2899  In the adjudicatory context, the Court has treated the availability of 
  2900  review by a superior executive officer as a significant feature 
  2901  distinguishing inferior officers from principal officers. Id. at 665.
  2902      That principle is particularly relevant where subordinate 
  2903  adjudicators exercise significant authority under Federal law. The 
  2904  Supreme Court has held that officials who occupy continuing offices and 
  2905  exercise significant discretion in conducting adjudications may be 
  2906  ``Officers of the United States'' rather than mere employees. See 
  2907  Freytag v. Comm'r, 501 U.S. 868, 881-82 (1991); Lucia v. SEC, 585 U.S. 
  2908  237, 245-51 (2018). The rule preserves supervision by the Director, a 
  2909  principal officer, before OPM's decision becomes final. Consistent with 
  2910  Freytag, Lucia, and related precedents, the Director will appoint, or 
  2911  ratify the appointments of, the OPM personnel assigned to adjudicate 
  2912  appeals under this subpart, ensuring that any adjudicator who exercises 
  2913  significant authority as an inferior officer has been properly 
  2914  appointed.
  2915      The Supreme Court's decision in United States v. Arthrex, 594 U.S. 
  2916  1, 22-23 (2021), confirms the importance of that structure. There, the 
  2917  Court held that administrative patent judges could not constitutionally 
  2918  issue unreviewable final decisions on behalf of the Executive Branch 
  2919  while being appointed only as inferior officers. The constitutional 
  2920  problem was not that subordinate adjudicators participated in deciding 
  2921  cases; it was that their decisions were insulated from review by
  2922  
  2923  [[Page 49253]]
  2924  
  2925  a principal officer. Id. at 25-26. The Court's remedy was to permit 
  2926  discretionary review by the Director of the Patent and Trademark 
  2927  Office, explaining that the Director need not review every decision, 
  2928  but must have authority to review decisions if he chooses. Id. at 27-
  2929  28.

Q8.answer: (a) Today, §351.806’s existing rule says an employee remains in duty status during the notice period “when possible”; the emergency lack-of-work-or-funds provisions separately address annual leave, LWOP, and nonpay status. The adopted but not-yet-effective text says “under ordinary circumstances” the employee remains in duty status and permits administrative leave for all or part of the period if appropriate and consistent with part 630, subpart N. It takes effect November 18, 2026. (b) Under the adopted text, employee consent is not specified as a condition: §630.1403(c)(10) authorizes administrative leave for an involuntary RIF during the interval from receipt of notice to separation when the agency determines it is in the Government’s best interests; OPM says “provide” includes leave with or without consent. The RIF-notice-period authority can cover all or part of that period; the text sets no separate numeric cap for this use. (c) OPM says its July 2025 Agency Policy Template already allowed an authorized agency official to provide administrative leave between receipt of an involuntary-separation notice and its effective date. OPM describes the new text as clarification of that policy and the existing “when possible” duty-status rule. (d) No. Administrative leave does not suspend other RIF requirements. OPM says retention registers, standing, veterans’ preference, notice and appeal rights continue; standing is fixed under §351.507 by receipt of the specific notice.
Q8.uncertainty: The October 26 placement occurred before the final rule’s November 18 effective date; the future text cannot itself govern that date. OPM’s pre-existing policy statement is preamble description of OPM guidance, not the adopted text.

Q9.answer: 1. **Not compliant.** The area was established 57 days before notice (within 90 days); it had to be submitted to OPM with a bona fide organizational-basis explanation for prior approval. The designee also must not be below headquarters. Require OPM approval in advance. 2. **In order.** Novak is serving an initial competitive-service probationary period and is not a competing employee; the agency may retain her while releasing a competing employee. 3. **Not compliant.** Ortiz’s supervisory probation is not an initial probationary period. As a career employee she must be included and ranked; require inclusion on the register. 4. **Not compliant.** Thirty days before October 13 is September 13. The October 2 rating is after the cutoff and cannot be used; recalculate without it. 5. **Not compliant.** Proxy=(7+5)/2=6; credit=7+5+6=18, not 15. 6. **Not compliant.** All employees are under a five-level pattern; the §351.503(d) extra-credit option is limited to patterns whose highest level is 3. Remove the blanket two points. 7. **In order.** With identical augmented credit, subgroup, and SCD (and same tenure group), the agency may select any tied employee for release. 8. **Not compliant.** The agency may not release a competing employee while retaining an employee on a specifically limited temporary or term promotion in that level. It must end/avoid that prohibited retention or not release the competing employee. 9. **In order on these facts.** Because Silva occupied the same position and earned L4 within the five-year period ending on receipt of his notice, an assessment is not required. 10. **Not compliant.** A self-rating questionnaire scored automatically cannot be the sole or principal qualification assessment. Use a job-analysis-based assessment demonstrating job-related skills, abilities, knowledge, and competencies. 11. **Not compliant.** Temporary exceptions under §351.608 stand alone and may not be stacked. Choose one applicable exception, subject to its limits; an exception over 30 days also requires written notice to higher-standing employees and a register entry of reasons and projected end date. 12. **Not compliant.** For notices issued after September 2, the notice must identify OPM, the filing deadline, and OPM’s electronic filing system—not MSPB and not merely a 30-day post-effective-date statement.
Q9.uncertainty: Step 8’s result assumes Reyes’s temporary promotion is the specifically limited promotion described in §351.602(a).

Q10.answer: (a) On September 10, the published amendment to §330.602(1) contained only the revised introductory text: a current competitive-service employee in the competitive service tenure group, GS-15 or below (or another OPM-qualifying appointment), “who:”. The two conditions that should have followed were inadvertently omitted, leaving the definition incomplete. (b) On September 15, 2026-18800 restored (1)(i) (RIF separation notice, without declining a qualifying same-schedule offer at least as high in representative rate) and (1)(ii) (proposed removal notice for declining a directed geographic relocation outside the local commuting area). OPM invoked good cause to skip notice and comment because it characterized the correction as no substantive change: it restored text in force before September 2 that OPM did not intend to remove or discuss removing. (c) A lower representative-rate full-time offer does not meet the test in (1)(i), so declining it does not defeat displaced status under that clause. A same-rate full-time offer is at least as high; declining it defeats displaced status under (1)(i), assuming the other stated conditions.
Q10.basis: 2026-15665, 91 FR 49217; correction 2026-18800, 91 FR 58363–58364, especially the correction’s description of the omission and restored text.
Q10.uncertainty: This answers only displaced status under §330.602(1)(i); other eligibility conditions or definitions are not at issue.

Q11.answer: Differences in the **regulatory amendments** (not preamble explanations) include: (1) §351.202(d): the proposal excluded categories from part 351 and allowed actions without regard to it; the final says they are not competing employees, adds conditions requiring actions to comply with appointment terms/law, and requires modified written notice for specified actions. (2) Competitive temporary/short-term appointment exclusions: proposal included temporary or term appointments ≤1 year under parts 316, subparts C or D; final limits the competitive-service exclusion to temporary appointments under subpart D and adds detailed notice provisions. (3) §351.203: final adds “restoration protected employee”; the proposal did not. The furlough definition drops the proposal’s added condition that emergency shutdown duration be dependent entirely on Congress rather than agency action. The final changes the Rating of Record cross-reference from §430.208(d) to (e), and adds the historical “prior to the final rule” qualifier for old pattern D systems. (4) §351.204: final adds the requirement to apply part 351 consistently with applicable laws, including 5 U.S.C. 2301(b); proposal only required following and applying part 351. (5) §351.302(d): final adds other procedures required by law, regulation, or appointment terms where applicable; proposal referred only to part 752. Final also recasts the canvass-letter language to address each employee individually. (6) §351.402: final adds paragraph (c), requiring advance OPM approval for a competitive area established or materially modified within 90 days before notices. (7) §351.502: proposal fixed tenure subgroup status as of notice issuance; final uses the date the employee receives the notice. Final also narrows the temporary appointment exclusion in §351.502(a)(3) to part 316 subpart D. (8) §351.504(a): proposal said veteran subgroups “should” be identified; final says they “must” be identified. (9) §351.505(b)(2): final corrects the proposal’s cross-reference from §351.503(b) to §351.504(b). (10) §351.506(d): final adds that absence of a right under this section does not limit access under another statute or regulation. (11) §351.604: the proposal revised furlough criteria and removed paragraph (d); the final did not adopt these changes. (12) §351.605: final separates notice requirements into paragraph (c) and explicitly states no register is required and assignment rights must not be applied in paragraph (d); proposal combined notice and no-assignment provisions in (b). (13) §351.606(a): final replaces the proposal’s simple priority rule with a detailed restoration-protection procedure, including first determining ordinary standing, not releasing a protected employee while another can be released, reassignment if no one else can be released, OPM placement assistance in specified cases, and documentation. The proposal also cited §351.209(b); final cites §353.209(b). (14) §351.608(a)(2): CTAP cross-reference changes from part 330, subpart E, to subpart F. (15) §351.701(a): “minimally successful” becomes “minimally satisfactory”; final adds “General.” and explicitly clarifies that promotion potential is not considered. (16) §351.702(a)(4): final changes the automated-self-assessment test to “does not consist solely of, or principally rely on” one and adds §351.702(a)(4)(v), waiving a new assessment in the stated five-year recent-successful-performance situation. (17) §351.802: final adds an introductory notice requirement, changes “veteran status” to “veterans’ preference subgroup,” and changes “link to part 351/access to records” to link to 5 CFR part 351 plus information on how to access records. (18) §351.805(b): final adds the later-only amended-notice rule; the proposal did not amend it.
Q11.basis: Comparison of proposed regulatory amendments 2026-04377, 91 FR 10926–10934, with final amendments 2026-15665, 91 FR 49218–49227. Corrections are reflected in 2026-17335, 91 FR 54794–54796.
Q11.uncertainty: The list focuses on substantive or operative differences, including materially changed cross-references; it omits punctuation, capitalization, and obvious grammatical corrections.

Q12.answer: (a) GS-13 register, using L5=7, L4=5, L3=3, L2=0 and the §351.503(f) missing-rating rules: Alvarez 7+7+5=19, preference 0, total 19, subgroup I. Brandt 3+5+0=8, preference 5, total 13, subgroup I/AD. Q13.answer: Examples of checked preamble/text discrepancies in 2026-15665: (1) **Erosion-of-duties trigger/section.** Preamble says OPM modifies §351.201(a)(2) to remove a post-announcement/within-180-days trigger (91 FR 49190, 1548–53); the amendatory text leaves §351.201(a)(2) in place and revises §351.202(c)(3) to bar an adverse erosion reclassification between formal RIF announcement and completion (91 FR 49218, 4896–4902). A later preamble passage correctly describes the new bar (91 FR 49190–49191, 1577–80). (2) **Transfer-of-function paragraph.** Preamble says §351.302(b) is revised to require part 752 or other procedures for a decliner’s separation (91 FR 49194, 2120–28); regulatory text places that requirement in §351.302(d) (91 FR 49219, 5091–96). No correction of that paragraph number elsewhere located. (3) **Temporary promotion/appointment.** Preamble says §351.602 removes a prohibition concerning a “specifically limited temporary appointment” (91 FR 49202, 2840–44); regulatory text concerns a “specifically limited temporary or term promotion” (91 FR 49223, 5620–27). No other passage appears to correct that description. (4) **Issuance versus receipt for standing.** A safeguards passage says standing is frozen on the date the RIF notice “is issued” (91 FR 49185, 904–11); §351.507(a) fixes it on the date the employee “receives” the specific notice (91 FR 49222, 5576–82). A later implementation passage correctly states receipt (91 FR 49207, 3413–16). (5) **Multiple-pattern enhanced-credit criteria.** Preamble says transmutation across patterns uses criteria in §351.503(d) (91 FR 49198, 2438–47), whose text includes special-act/service awards; §351.503(e)(1)(i), the operative multiple-pattern rule, instead lists highest agency/departmental award, QSI, or appraisal awards/bonuses and does not list special-act/service awards (91 FR 49221–49222, 5373–94). No clear preamble correction located. (6) **Three-grade assignment limit.** Detailed assignment discussion states without qualification that positions must be no more than three grades below (91 FR 49204, 3064–69); §351.701(b)(2) allows five grades for a preference eligible with a 30-percent disability (91 FR 49225, 5894–5909). The executive summary correctly notes the five-grade exception (91 FR 49178, 161–67). (7) **Assessment standard.** Preamble describes an assessment that “does not rely on a self-assessment from an automated examination” (91 FR 49204, 3081–86); §351.702(a)(4)(iii) allows an assessment that does not consist solely of, or principally rely on, an automated self-assessment (91 FR 49226, 5985–6000). The operative text allows limited nonprincipal reliance; no precise preamble correction located.
Q13.basis: Preamble and regulatory-text page/line references within 2026-15665 are provided item by item above.
Q13.uncertainty: The assessment item is a difference in phrasing and scope; the preamble may have intended shorthand rather than a categorical prohibition. The other listed differences are direct paragraph, trigger, or category mismatches.

Q14.answer: (i) **OPM preamble versus final text:** (1) The final rule’s DATES/preamble says OPM’s appeal process applies only when the specific RIF notice was issued on or after September 2, 2026 (2026-15666, 91 FR 49230, 83–85; 49247–49248, 2418–28). But regulatory §351.901(a) contains no notice-date transition and facially grants an OPM appeal to any employee subjected to a covered RIF action (91 FR 49263, 4264–68). The preamble expressly acknowledges no applicability note was included in the regulatory text. (2) Preamble says the rule does not retroactively invalidate existing CBAs and leaves particular existing-agreement disputes to chapter 71 forums (91 FR 49245, 1997–2007); operative §351.901(c)(2) says a RIF action and any matter relating to its appeal may not be raised in a negotiated grievance procedure or grievance arbitration, without an express existing-CBA exception (91 FR 49263–49264, 4279–95). (3) Section-by-section preamble says service of appeal information is subject to disclosure limits in §351.903(b) (91 FR 49250, 2627–33); final §351.903(e) states its own disclosure limitations, while §351.903(b)(4) governs the agency’s service of the record (91 FR 49265, 4443–49, 4463–71). (ii) Proposal-to-final changes not clearly acknowledged in the final rule’s change summary include: §351.902(a) changes reconsideration “of an initial appeal” to reconsideration “of an initial decision” (proposal 2026-02576, 91 FR 5874, 1936–41; final 2026-15666, 91 FR 49264, 4302–07); §351.902(c)(2) adds an exception allowing filing/access by a person exempted from e-filer registration under (c)(7), absent from proposal (proposal 91 FR 5875, 1961–65; final 91 FR 49264, 4334–42); §351.905(c) deletes the proposal’s express power to require “any other appropriate action” in addition to a hearing, replacing it with the narrower hearing language and separate information/audit authority (proposal 91 FR 5876, 2091–2103; final 91 FR 49265–49266, 4532–58); §351.906(b) changes mandatory “shall” sanctions to discretionary “may” (proposal 91 FR 5877, 2145–54; final 91 FR 49266, 4590–99); and final §351.906(c) adds a sanction proportionality/causal-relation limit (91 FR 49266, 4600–02), not identified in the summary. The final also omits the proposal’s express statement that the OPM process “shall supersede” agency-policy and CBA appeal procedures; the summary describes exclusivity and the grievance bar but does not identify that deletion (proposal 91 FR 5875, 1922–31; final 91 FR 49263–49264, 4279–95). (iii) The Board’s rule retains only Foreign Service RIF appeals in its regulatory text, while its preamble says it will still hear legacy pending/new non-Foreign-Service RIF appeals (2026-16456, 91 FR 51998, 115–40, 180–87; regulatory text, 91 FR 51998, 269–99). The transition triggers also conflict: Board preamble says in one passage it will accept post-September 2 cases where the RIF notice was issued before that date (91 FR 51998, 130–40), but elsewhere says it will hear new cases only where the RIF effective date preceded September 2 (91 FR 51998, 180–84). OPM’s rule uses notice issuance—not effective date—as the dividing line (2026-15666, 91 FR 49230, 83–85).
Q14.uncertainty: The CBA tension is between operative text and the preamble’s treatment of existing agreements; the Federal Register does not resolve how a particular existing agreement would be treated. The Board’s transition passages state competing criteria, and the regulatory text itself does not codify the legacy-case exception.

Q1.answer: (a) The main final rule is 2026-15665, *Reduction in Force*, 91 FR 49178–49227, published August 3, 2026, effective September 2, 2026; Docket OPM-2025-0107; RIN 3206-AO86. (b) Its proposal is 2026-04377, 91 FR 10904–10934, published March 5, 2026. (c) Two corrections through November 14: 2026-17335, published August 25, effective September 2, corrected typographical and clerical errors in amendatory instructions and regulatory text; and 2026-18800, published and effective September 15, restored two inadvertently omitted subparagraphs in the CTAP definition of “displaced” in 5 CFR 330.602. (d) The amended RIF rules govern RIFs for which the agency issues a RIF notice on or after September 2, 2026. A notice issued before that date means the RIF is processed under the rules in force when the notice was issued. (e) Other 2026 final rules amending part 351 with effect on or after September 2: 2026-15666, *Reduction in Force Appeals*, effective September 2 and in force today; it replaces the OPM appeal process and revises notice requirements. 2026-21320, *Administrative Leave for Workforce Realignment and Other Purposes*, effective November 18, not yet in force today; it revises §351.806 on status during a RIF notice period. The appeals correction 2026-17338 is excluded as a correction, as requested.

Q3.answer: (a) A: not preference eligible; 0 points; subgroup B. His 22 years of length-of-service retirement and rank alone do not satisfy §351.504(b)(1)–(3), and he is not a disabled veteran for (b)(4). B: not preference eligible; 0 points; subgroup B. Although disabled and a commander, the stated 21-year length-of-service retirement does not meet (b)(1) or (b)(2); he also fails (b)(3), and rank-major-or-above clause (b)(4) still requires one of (b)(1)–(3). C: preference eligible; 5 points; subgroup AD. Disability retirement directly resulting from line-of-duty armed conflict meets (b)(1)(i), and the 40-percent disability meets (a)(1). D: not preference eligible; 0 points; subgroup B. Twenty-four years of length-of-service retirement and enlisted rank do not meet (b)(1)–(3). E: preference eligible; 3 points; subgroup A. Retired pay not based on 20 or more years meets (b)(2); 10-percent disability does not qualify for the 5-point category. C is preference eligible under 5 U.S.C. 2108 and §351.504(b), so all 14 years are creditable under §351.505(b)(2)(ii); September 7, 2010 minus 14 years is September 7, 1996. Q5.answer: (a) (i) The August 28 notice is before September 2, so the earlier rules apply even though the RIF is effective October 27. In OPM’s own old-rule examples, three Level 3 ratings yield 12 years of additional service credit and three Level 5 ratings yield 20. Lee’s adjusted SCD is March 2, 1998 minus 12 years = March 2, 1986; Park’s is July 8, 2019 minus 20 years = July 8, 1999. Same tenure and nonpreference subgroup; Lee is retained, Park released. (ii) and (iii) Notices September 2 and September 3 are both on/after the effective date. New scores: Lee 3+3+3=9; Park 7+7+7=21. Park retained; Lee released. (b) No. An amended notice solely moving the effective date later does not require recalculation. Lee’s October 15 rating does not change standing fixed at the original notice. (c) Version of rules: date the agency issues the specific notice. Four-year ratings window: the notice-issuance date, or the agency cutoff date if one is used. Tenure subgroup and retention standing: the date the employee receives the specific notice. A later-only amended notice does not restart standing.

Q6.answer: (a) Jordan qualifies for assignment rights (current annual L2). He may be assigned to positions in the same competitive area and full-time schedule, held by lower-standing employees in the same tenure group, within three one-grade intervals below GS-13. GS-12 Ellis, GS-11 Frank, and GS-10 Gale qualify; GS-9 Hana is four intervals down; GS-12 Ito has higher standing; Kim’s position is part-time; Lund is in another competitive area. Of the available positions, GS-12 Ellis requires the least reduction in representative rate and must be offered. (b) With the 30-percent disability, the limit becomes five intervals, so Hana’s GS-9 position also becomes eligible; GS-12 Ellis remains the least-reduction offer. (c) With current annual L1, no assignment right under §351.701(a), which requires L2 or higher. (d) If all are excepted-service employees, assignment rights are not mandatory under §351.701(a); an agency may adopt them under §351.705(a). No adopted agency policy is stated. (e) The 2026 rule removed the old Level-2 bar on assignment to a position held by a higher-rated employee. Assignment depends on the holder’s lower retention standing and the regulatory grade, schedule, area, and qualification requirements, not a comparison of incumbent ratings. “Bumping” and “retreating” are no longer separate rights; the preamble describes the replacement as one assignment standard to a lower-standing holder.
Q6.basis: 5 CFR 351.701(a)–(d), (f), and 351.705(a), 91 FR 49225–49226. The deletion of former §351.701(d) and elimination of bump/retreat are explained at 2026-15665, 91 FR 49204.
Q6.uncertainty: The excepted-service result depends on whether the agency has adopted optional assignment provisions; none are specified.

Q7.answer: (a) MSPB. The notice was issued August 31, before the September 2 transition date; the later October 30 effective date does not move the appeal to OPM. (b) OPM. Morgan must file in the OPM electronic filing system identified on OPM’s website, unless OPM grants a good-cause filing exemption. Count December 19 as day 1; December 31 is day 13; January 17, 2027 is day 30. Because January 17 is Sunday and January 18 is a Federal holiday, the deadline extends to Tuesday, January 19, 2027, 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time. (c) By a preponderance, she must prove timeliness, OPM jurisdiction, agency failure to comply with an applicable RIF statute or OPM regulation, and prejudice—i.e., the failure caused the appealed action or loss of a materially more favorable outcome. No hearing is guaranteed; OPM uses the written record unless a hearing is necessary and efficient to resolve material facts or a material credibility dispute. (d) The regulatory text makes part 351 the exclusive direct appeal process and bars raising a RIF action or related appeal matter through a negotiated grievance procedure or grievance arbitration. The preamble says it does not retroactively invalidate existing CBAs and leaves questions about particular existing provisions to the appropriate chapter 71 forum. (e) No judicial review of an OPM decision under this subpart. (f) Yes, if the OSC matter was timely filed before the original deadline and the final decision materially affects her part 351 rights. March 11 is day 1 after March 10; day 30 is April 9, 2027. She may file through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time that day. (g) The controlling transition criterion is the agency’s issuance of the specific RIF notice on or after September 2, 2026, not the effective date of separation.
Q7.basis: OPM final appeal rule 2026-15666, DATES, 91 FR 49230; 5 CFR 351.901–.905, 91 FR 49263–49265. The CBA explanation is 2026-15666, 91 FR 49244–49245. MSPB transition explanation: 2026-16456, 91 FR 51997–51998. OPM’s proposal, not final authority, is 2026-02576, 91 FR 5861–5877; correction 2026-17338, 91 FR 54796.
Q7.uncertainty: The rule assigns OPM sole discretion to determine good cause and whether a collateral final decision materially affects part 351 rights.

Q8.answer: (a) Today, §351.806’s existing rule says an employee remains in duty status during the notice period “when possible”; the emergency lack-of-work-or-funds provisions separately address annual leave, LWOP, and nonpay status. The adopted but not-yet-effective text says “under ordinary circumstances” the employee remains in duty status and permits administrative leave for all or part of the period if appropriate and consistent with part 630, subpart N. It takes effect November 18, 2026. (b) Under the adopted text, employee consent is not specified as a condition: §630.1403(c)(10) authorizes administrative leave for an involuntary RIF during the interval from receipt of notice to separation when the agency determines it is in the Government’s best interests; OPM says “provide” includes leave with or without consent. The RIF-notice-period authority can cover all or part of that period; the text sets no separate numeric cap for this use. (c) OPM says its July 2025 Agency Policy Template already allowed an authorized agency official to provide administrative leave between receipt of an involuntary-separation notice and its effective date. OPM describes the new text as clarification of that policy and the existing “when possible” duty-status rule. (d) No. Administrative leave does not suspend other RIF requirements. OPM says retention registers, standing, veterans’ preference, notice and appeal rights continue; standing is fixed under §351.507 by receipt of the specific notice.
Q8.uncertainty: The October 26 placement occurred before the final rule’s November 18 effective date; the future text cannot itself govern that date. OPM’s pre-existing policy statement is preamble description of OPM guidance, not the adopted text.

Q9.answer: 1. **Not compliant.** The area was established 57 days before notice (within 90 days); it had to be submitted to OPM with a bona fide organizational-basis explanation for prior approval. The designee also must not be below headquarters. Require OPM approval in advance. 2. **In order.** Novak is serving an initial competitive-service probationary period and is not a competing employee; the agency may retain her while releasing a competing employee. 3. **Not compliant.** Ortiz’s supervisory probation is not an initial probationary period. As a career employee she must be included and ranked; require inclusion on the register. 4. **Not compliant.** Thirty days before October 13 is September 13. The October 2 rating is after the cutoff and cannot be used; recalculate without it. 5. **Not compliant.** Proxy=(7+5)/2=6; credit=7+5+6=18, not 15. 6. **Not compliant.** All employees are under a five-level pattern; the §351.503(d) extra-credit option is limited to patterns whose highest level is 3. Remove the blanket two points. 7. **In order.** With identical augmented credit, subgroup, and SCD (and same tenure group), the agency may select any tied employee for release. 8. **Not compliant.** The agency may not release a competing employee while retaining an employee on a specifically limited temporary or term promotion in that level. It must end/avoid that prohibited retention or not release the competing employee. 9. **In order on these facts.** Because Silva occupied the same position and earned L4 within the five-year period ending on receipt of his notice, an assessment is not required. 10. **Not compliant.** A self-rating questionnaire scored automatically cannot be the sole or principal qualification assessment. Use a job-analysis-based assessment demonstrating job-related skills, abilities, knowledge, and competencies. 11. **Not compliant.** Temporary exceptions under §351.608 stand alone and may not be stacked. Choose one applicable exception, subject to its limits; an exception over 30 days also requires written notice to higher-standing employees and a register entry of reasons and projected end date. 12. **Not compliant.** For notices issued after September 2, the notice must identify OPM, the filing deadline, and OPM’s electronic filing system—not MSPB and not merely a 30-day post-effective-date statement.
Q9.uncertainty: Step 8’s result assumes Reyes’s temporary promotion is the specifically limited promotion described in §351.602(a).

Q10.answer: (a) On September 10, the published amendment to §330.602(1) contained only the revised introductory text: a current competitive-service employee in the competitive service tenure group, GS-15 or below (or another OPM-qualifying appointment), “who:”. The two conditions that should have followed were inadvertently omitted, leaving the definition incomplete. (b) On September 15, 2026-18800 restored (1)(i) (RIF separation notice, without declining a qualifying same-schedule offer at least as high in representative rate) and (1)(ii) (proposed removal notice for declining a directed geographic relocation outside the local commuting area). OPM invoked good cause to skip notice and comment because it characterized the correction as no substantive change: it restored text in force before September 2 that OPM did not intend to remove or discuss removing. (c) A lower representative-rate full-time offer does not meet the test in (1)(i), so declining it does not defeat displaced status under that clause. A same-rate full-time offer is at least as high; declining it defeats displaced status under (1)(i), assuming the other stated conditions.
Q10.basis: 2026-15665, 91 FR 49217; correction 2026-18800, 91 FR 58363–58364, especially the correction’s description of the omission and restored text.
Q10.uncertainty: This answers only displaced status under §330.602(1)(i); other eligibility conditions or definitions are not at issue.

Q11.answer: Differences in the **regulatory amendments** (not preamble explanations) include: (1) §351.202(d): the proposal excluded categories from part 351 and allowed actions without regard to it; the final says they are not competing employees, adds conditions requiring actions to comply with appointment terms/law, and requires modified written notice for specified actions. (2) Competitive temporary/short-term appointment exclusions: proposal included temporary or term appointments ≤1 year under parts 316, subparts C or D; final limits the competitive-service exclusion to temporary appointments under subpart D and adds detailed notice provisions. (3) §351.203: final adds “restoration protected employee”; the proposal did not. The furlough definition drops the proposal’s added condition that emergency shutdown duration be dependent entirely on Congress rather than agency action. The final changes the Rating of Record cross-reference from §430.208(d) to (e), and adds the historical “prior to the final rule” qualifier for old pattern D systems. (4) §351.204: final adds the requirement to apply part 351 consistently with applicable laws, including 5 U.S.C. 2301(b); proposal only required following and applying part 351. (5) §351.302(d): final adds other procedures required by law, regulation, or appointment terms where applicable; proposal referred only to part 752. Final also recasts the canvass-letter language to address each employee individually. (6) §351.402: final adds paragraph (c), requiring advance OPM approval for a competitive area established or materially modified within 90 days before notices. (7) §351.502: proposal fixed tenure subgroup status as of notice issuance; final uses the date the employee receives the notice. Final also narrows the temporary appointment exclusion in §351.502(a)(3) to part 316 subpart D. (8) §351.504(a): proposal said veteran subgroups “should” be identified; final says they “must” be identified. (9) §351.505(b)(2): final corrects the proposal’s cross-reference from §351.503(b) to §351.504(b). (10) §351.506(d): final adds that absence of a right under this section does not limit access under another statute or regulation. (11) §351.604: the proposal revised furlough criteria and removed paragraph (d); the final did not adopt these changes. (12) §351.605: final separates notice requirements into paragraph (c) and explicitly states no register is required and assignment rights must not be applied in paragraph (d); proposal combined notice and no-assignment provisions in (b). (13) §351.606(a): final replaces the proposal’s simple priority rule with a detailed restoration-protection procedure, including first determining ordinary standing, not releasing a protected employee while another can be released, reassignment if no one else can be released, OPM placement assistance in specified cases, and documentation. The proposal also cited §351.209(b); final cites §353.209(b). (14) §351.608(a)(2): CTAP cross-reference changes from part 330, subpart E, to subpart F. (15) §351.701(a): “minimally successful” becomes “minimally satisfactory”; final adds “General.” and explicitly clarifies that promotion potential is not considered. (16) §351.702(a)(4): final changes the automated-self-assessment test to “does not consist solely of, or principally rely on” one and adds §351.702(a)(4)(v), waiving a new assessment in the stated five-year recent-successful-performance situation. (17) §351.802: final adds an introductory notice requirement, changes “veteran status” to “veterans’ preference subgroup,” and changes “link to part 351/access to records” to link to 5 CFR part 351 plus information on how to access records. (18) §351.805(b): final adds the later-only amended-notice rule; the proposal did not amend it.
Q11.basis: Comparison of proposed regulatory amendments 2026-04377, 91 FR 10926–10934, with final amendments 2026-15665, 91 FR 49218–49227. Corrections are reflected in 2026-17335, 91 FR 54794–54796.
Q11.uncertainty: The list focuses on substantive or operative differences, including materially changed cross-references; it omits punctuation, capitalization, and obvious grammatical corrections.

Q12.answer: (a) GS-13 register, using L5=7, L4=5, L3=3, L2=0 and the §351.503(f) missing-rating rules: Alvarez 7+7+5=19, preference 0, total 19, subgroup I. Brandt 3+5+0=8, preference 5, total 13, subgroup I/AD. Chen’s September 30, 2022 L2 is outside the four years before October 5, 2026; the two eligible ratings are 7 and 5, proxy=(7+5)/2=6; 7+5+6=18, preference 0, subgroup I. Dube: 5+5+5=15, preference 3, total 18, subgroup II because initial probation ended. Estrada’s October 20, 2026 L5 is after the notice; eligible ratings are 5+3+5=13, preference 3, total 16, subgroup I. Farouk’s one L3 is 3×3=9, preference 0; subgroup I. Quinn is excluded from competition because she is serving an initial probationary period, so is not on the register. Order: Alvarez 19; Chen 18 (subgroup I); Dube 18 (subgroup II); Estrada 16; Brandt 13; Farouk 9. (b) Farouk’s 14-month uniformed service gives one year of restoration protection; restored July 13, 2026, he is still within it on October 5. The agency must retain him as a mandatory exception while other competing employees may be released. With three GS-13 positions abolished, the three releases are Dube, Estrada, and Brandt, passing over protected Farouk. Quinn may be retained without competition. (c) Dube’s assignment choices among lower-standing holders in the same tenure group and within three one-grade intervals are Hill (GS-11), Jones (GS-10), and Ikeda (GS-9); Gomez (GS-12) has higher standing. Least reduction: Hill’s GS-11. Estrada can take lower-standing Jones (GS-10) or Ikeda (GS-9), but not Gomez (higher standing); with Hill allocated to Dube, the least-reduction available position is Jones (GS-10). Brandt’s 30-percent disability extends the limit to five intervals; Gomez, Hill, and Jones have higher standing, while Ikeda has lower standing, so Brandt must be offered GS-9 Ikeda. Same area/full-time schedule and stated qualifications are satisfied. (d) If accepted, Dube, Estrada, and Brandt occupy Hill’s, Jones’s, and Ikeda’s positions; those incumbents are displaced and, under the stated assumption that each is qualified only for the held position, are separated. The three remaining agency separations are Hill, Jones, and Ikeda.
Q12.uncertainty: The assignment provisions do not expressly set out a general cascading-assignment procedure in the printed text. The stated displacement/separation result assumes each displaced incumbent receives no further qualifying assignment, consistent with the scenario’s qualification limits.

Q13.answer: Examples of checked preamble/text discrepancies in 2026-15665: (1) **Erosion-of-duties trigger/section.** Preamble says OPM modifies §351.201(a)(2) to remove a post-announcement/within-180-days trigger (91 FR 49190, 1548–53); the amendatory text leaves §351.201(a)(2) in place and revises §351.202(c)(3) to bar an adverse erosion reclassification between formal RIF announcement and completion (91 FR 49218, 4896–4902). A later preamble passage correctly describes the new bar (91 FR 49190–49191, 1577–80). (2) **Transfer-of-function paragraph.** Preamble says §351.302(b) is revised to require part 752 or other procedures for a decliner’s separation (91 FR 49194, 2120–28); regulatory text places that requirement in §351.302(d) (91 FR 49219, 5091–96). No correction of that paragraph number elsewhere located. (3) **Temporary promotion/appointment.** Preamble says §351.602 removes a prohibition concerning a “specifically limited temporary appointment” (91 FR 49202, 2840–44); regulatory text concerns a “specifically limited temporary or term promotion” (91 FR 49223, 5620–27). No other passage appears to correct that description. (4) **Issuance versus receipt for standing.** A safeguards passage says standing is frozen on the date the RIF notice “is issued” (91 FR 49185, 904–11); §351.507(a) fixes it on the date the employee “receives” the specific notice (91 FR 49222, 5576–82). A later implementation passage correctly states receipt (91 FR 49207, 3413–16). (5) **Multiple-pattern enhanced-credit criteria.** Preamble says transmutation across patterns uses criteria in §351.503(d) (91 FR 49198, 2438–47), whose text includes special-act/service awards; §351.503(e)(1)(i), the operative multiple-pattern rule, instead lists highest agency/departmental award, QSI, or appraisal awards/bonuses and does not list special-act/service awards (91 FR 49221–49222, 5373–94). No clear preamble correction located. (6) **Three-grade assignment limit.** Detailed assignment discussion states without qualification that positions must be no more than three grades below (91 FR 49204, 3064–69); §351.701(b)(2) allows five grades for a preference eligible with a 30-percent disability (91 FR 49225, 5894–5909). The executive summary correctly notes the five-grade exception (91 FR 49178, 161–67). (7) **Assessment standard.** Preamble describes an assessment that “does not rely on a self-assessment from an automated examination” (91 FR 49204, 3081–86); §351.702(a)(4)(iii) allows an assessment that does not consist solely of, or principally rely on, an automated self-assessment (91 FR 49226, 5985–6000). The operative text allows limited nonprincipal reliance; no precise preamble correction located.
Q13.basis: Preamble and regulatory-text page/line references within 2026-15665 are provided item by item above.
Q13.uncertainty: The assessment item is a difference in phrasing and scope; the preamble may have intended shorthand rather than a categorical prohibition. The other listed differences are direct paragraph, trigger, or category mismatches.

Q14.answer: (i) **OPM preamble versus final text:** (1) The final rule’s DATES/preamble says OPM’s appeal process applies only when the specific RIF notice was issued on or after September 2, 2026 (2026-15666, 91 FR 49230, 83–85; 49247–49248, 2418–28). But regulatory §351.901(a) contains no notice-date transition and facially grants an OPM appeal to any employee subjected to a covered RIF action (91 FR 49263, 4264–68). The preamble expressly acknowledges no applicability note was included in the regulatory text. (2) Preamble says the rule does not retroactively invalidate existing CBAs and leaves particular existing-agreement disputes to chapter 71 forums (91 FR 49245, 1997–2007); operative §351.901(c)(2) says a RIF action and any matter relating to its appeal may not be raised in a negotiated grievance procedure or grievance arbitration, without an express existing-CBA exception (91 FR 49263–49264, 4279–95). (3) Section-by-section preamble says service of appeal information is subject to disclosure limits in §351.903(b) (91 FR 49250, 2627–33); final §351.903(e) states its own disclosure limitations, while §351.903(b)(4) governs the agency’s service of the record (91 FR 49265, 4443–49, 4463–71). (ii) Proposal-to-final changes not clearly acknowledged in the final rule’s change summary include: §351.902(a) changes reconsideration “of an initial appeal” to reconsideration “of an initial decision” (proposal 2026-02576, 91 FR 5874, 1936–41; final 2026-15666, 91 FR 49264, 4302–07); §351.902(c)(2) adds an exception allowing filing/access by a person exempted from e-filer registration under (c)(7), absent from proposal (proposal 91 FR 5875, 1961–65; final 91 FR 49264, 4334–42); §351.905(c) deletes the proposal’s express power to require “any other appropriate action” in addition to a hearing, replacing it with the narrower hearing language and separate information/audit authority (proposal 91 FR 5876, 2091–2103; final 91 FR 49265–49266, 4532–58); §351.906(b) changes mandatory “shall” sanctions to discretionary “may” (proposal 91 FR 5877, 2145–54; final 91 FR 49266, 4590–99); and final §351.906(c) adds a sanction proportionality/causal-relation limit (91 FR 49266, 4600–02), not identified in the summary. The final also omits the proposal’s express statement that the OPM process “shall supersede” agency-policy and CBA appeal procedures; the summary describes exclusivity and the grievance bar but does not identify that deletion (proposal 91 FR 5875, 1922–31; final 91 FR 49263–49264, 4279–95). (iii) The Board’s rule retains only Foreign Service RIF appeals in its regulatory text, while its preamble says it will still hear legacy pending/new non-Foreign-Service RIF appeals (2026-16456, 91 FR 51998, 115–40, 180–87; regulatory text, 91 FR 51998, 269–99). The transition triggers also conflict: Board preamble says in one passage it will accept post-September 2 cases where the RIF notice was issued before that date (91 FR 51998, 130–40), but elsewhere says it will hear new cases only where the RIF effective date preceded September 2 (91 FR 51998, 180–84). OPM’s rule uses notice issuance—not effective date—as the dividing line (2026-15666, 91 FR 49230, 83–85).
Q14.uncertainty: The CBA tension is between operative text and the preamble’s treatment of existing agreements; the Federal Register does not resolve how a particular existing agreement would be treated. The Board’s transition passages state competing criteria, and the regulatory text itself does not codify the legacy-case exception.
